relationship: parallel account of Hezekiah's response to the Assyrian report
rationale: Both describe Hezekiah hearing the report, tearing his garments, putting on sackcloth and entering the Lord's house. The preceding reports in both narratives concern the Assyrian envoy's words.
source_text: When King Hezekiah heard, he tore his garments, wrapped himself in sackcloth, and went up to the Lord’s house.

target_units.text: When King Hezekiah heard, he tore his garments, put on sackcloth, and entered the Lord’s house.

relationship: parallel delegation to Isaiah in sackcloth
rationale: Both name Eliakim the steward, Somnas the scribe and the priestly elders sent in sackcloth to Isaiah son of Amos. The specified messengers and purpose identify the same narrative episode.
source_text: He sent Eliakim the steward, Somnas the scribe, and the elders of the priests, wrapped in sackcloth, to the prophet Isaiah son of Amos.

target_units.text: He sent Eliakim the steward, Somnas the scribe, and the elders of the priests, clothed in sackcloth, to Isaiah the prophet, son of Amos.

relationship: close birth-pain image in Hezekiah's message
rationale: Both give Hezekiah's description of the crisis as a day of distress and rebuke and compare it to labor without strength to give birth. Isaiah additionally includes wrath in its description.
source_text: They said to him, “Thus says Hezekiah: Today is a day of distress, reproach, reproof, and wrath, for labor has come upon the woman giving birth, but she has no strength to give birth.

target_units.text: They said to him, ‘Thus says Hezekiah: This day is a day of affliction, rebuke, and provocation. Children have reached the birth pains, but the woman giving birth has no strength.

relationship: parallel appeal for prayer after reproach of the living God
rationale: Both ask that God hear the Assyrian envoy's reproach of the living God and request prayer for the remaining people. Their envoy's name appears as Rapsakes and Rhapsakes respectively.
source_text: May the Lord your God hear Rapsakes’ words, which the king of the Assyrians sent to reproach the living God and to reproach words that the Lord your God has heard. You shall plead with the Lord your God for those who remain.”

target_units.text: Perhaps the Lord your God will hear all Rhapsakes’s words, whom his master the king of the Assyrians sent to reproach the living God and to blaspheme with words which the Lord your God has heard. Take up a prayer for the remnant that remains.’

relationship: parallel arrival of Hezekiah's servants before Isaiah
rationale: Both record the king's servants coming to Isaiah between Hezekiah's appeal and the prophet's reply. The named king and prophet and matching narrative position make this a particular historical correspondence.
source_text: The king’s servants came to Isaiah,

target_units.text: King Hezekiah’s servants came to Isaiah.

relationship: parallel reassurance against the Assyrian envoys' words
rationale: Both instruct the messengers to tell their master not to fear the words spoken by Assyria's representatives against God. Kings calls the representatives young servants, while Isaiah calls them envoys.
source_text: and Isaiah said to them, “You shall say this to your master: Thus says the Lord: Do not fear the words you heard, with which the king of the Assyrians’ envoys reproached Me.

target_units.text: Isaiah said to them, ‘Tell your master: Thus says the Lord: Do not fear the words you have heard, with which the king of the Assyrians’ young servants blasphemed.

relationship: parallel prediction of the Assyrian king's return and death
rationale: Both announce a spirit placed within the king, a report he will hear, his return to his own land and his death there by the sword.
source_text: Behold, I will put a spirit into him. On hearing a report he will return to his country, and he will fall by the sword in his own land.”

target_units.text: Behold, I am putting a spirit within him. He shall hear a report and return to his land, and I shall bring him down by the sword in his land.’

relationship: parallel encounter with the Assyrian king at Lomna
rationale: Both describe the returning Assyrian envoy finding the king fighting or besieging Lomna. Kings also explains that he had heard of the departure from Lachish.
source_text: Rapsakes returned and found the king besieging Lomna. The king of the Assyrians heard that

target_units.text: Rhapsakes returned and found the king of the Assyrians fighting against Lomna, for he had heard that he had departed from Lachish.

relationship: parallel report of Tharaka and renewed messengers to Hezekiah
rationale: Both name Tharaka king of the Ethiopians coming against Assyria's king and describe the subsequent sending of messengers to Hezekiah. Isaiah speaks of besieging him; Kings speaks of fighting him.
source_text: Tharaka king of the Ethiopians had come out to besiege him. On hearing this he turned back and sent messengers to Hezekiah, saying,

target_units.text: He heard concerning Tharaka king of the Ethiopians, ‘Behold, he has come out to fight you.’ He returned and sent messengers to Hezekiah, saying,

relationship: parallel challenge to Hezekiah's trust in Jerusalem's deliverance
rationale: Both convey the Assyrian warning against trusting the promise that Jerusalem will not be handed to Assyria. Isaiah calls this being deceived, whereas Kings speaks of being lifted up by that assurance.
source_text: “You shall say this to Hezekiah king of Judea: Do not let your God, on whom you rely, deceive you by saying, ‘Jerusalem will certainly not be handed into the king of the Assyrians’ hands.’

target_units.text: ‘Do not let your God, in whom you trust, lift you up by saying, “Jerusalem will certainly not be handed into the hands of the king of the Assyrians.”

relationship: parallel Assyrian boast of widespread destruction
rationale: Both appeal to what Hezekiah has heard about the Assyrian kings' destruction of other lands. Kings then expressly challenges whether he will be rescued.
source_text: Or have you not heard what the kings of the Assyrians did—how they destroyed the whole earth?

target_units.text: Behold, you have heard everything the kings of the Assyrians did to all the lands, devoting them to destruction. And will you be rescued?

relationship: parallel catalogue of peoples whose gods did not rescue them
rationale: Both ask whether the gods of peoples destroyed by the speaker's fathers rescued them and name Gozan, Charran and Raphes. The additional geography differs: Isaiah names Themad, while Kings names Edem's sons in Thaesthen.
source_text: Did the gods of the nations my fathers destroyed rescue them—Gozan, Charran, and Raphes, which are in the country of Themad?

target_units.text: Did the gods of the nations my fathers destroyed rescue them—Gozan, Charran, Raphes, and the sons of Edem in Thaesthen?

relationship: parallel challenge concerning defeated cities and kings
rationale: Both ask where the rulers or cities named Aimath, Arphath or Arphad, Seppharim or Seppharouain, Anag or Ana, and Ougaua or Ava are. The matching challenge preserves the respective supplied name forms.
source_text: Where are the kings of Aimath and Arphath, and of the city of Seppharim, Anag, and Ougaua?”

target_units.text: Where are the king of Aimath and the king of Arphad? And where are Seppharouain, Ana, and Ava?’

relationship: parallel presentation of the Assyrian document before the Lord
rationale: Both describe Hezekiah receiving the messengers' document and opening or unfolding it before the Lord. Kings additionally expressly mentions reading the letters and going up to the Lord's house.
source_text: Hezekiah took the document from the messengers and opened it before the Lord.

target_units.text: Hezekiah took the letters from the messengers’ hand and read them. He went up to the Lord’s house, and Hezekiah unfolded them before the Lord.

relationship: parallel record of Hezekiah praying during the Assyrian crisis
rationale: Isaiah introduces Hezekiah's prayer to the Lord; Chronicles likewise records his prayer and cry to heaven during this crisis, also naming Isaiah as praying with him.
source_text: Hezekiah prayed to the Lord, saying,

target_units.text: King Hezekiah and Isaiah son of Amoz the prophet prayed about these things and cried out to heaven.

relationship: parallel confession of the cherubim-enthroned Creator
rationale: Both prayers address Israel's God seated upon the cherubim, confess Him alone as God of the earth's kingdoms and declare that He made heaven and earth.
source_text: “Lord Sabaoth, God of Israel, seated upon the cherubim, Thou alone art God of every kingdom of the inhabited world. Thou didst make heaven and earth.

target_units.text: He said, ‘Lord, Israel’s God, seated upon the cherubim, Thou alone art God among all the kingdoms of the earth. Thou madest heaven and earth.

relationship: parallel appeal that God attend to Sennacherib's reproach
rationale: Both ask the Lord to hear and see the words Sennacherib sent to reproach the living God. Kings develops the petition with the explicit images of God's ear and eyes.
source_text: Hear, Lord; look, Lord, and see the words that Sennacherib sent to reproach the living God.

target_units.text: Incline Thine ear, Lord, and hear. Open Thine eyes, Lord, and see. Hear Sennacherib’s words, which he sent to reproach the living God.

relationship: parallel acknowledgment of Assyria's actual devastation
rationale: Both prayers acknowledge that Assyria's kings truly devastated other territories before explaining why the destroyed idols were not gods. Isaiah uses the wider expression of the inhabited world and their country.
source_text: For the kings of the Assyrians have truly laid waste the whole inhabited world and their country,

target_units.text: For truly, Lord, the kings of the Assyrians have devastated the nations

relationship: parallel explanation of burned idols as human handiwork
rationale: Both explain that the idols cast into fire were not gods but human works made of wood and stone. Their destruction therefore supplies no proof against the living God addressed in the prayer.
source_text: and cast their idols into the fire. For they were not gods, but works of human hands, wood and stones, and they destroyed them.

target_units.text: and put their gods into the fire, for they are not gods but the work of human hands, wood and stones; so they destroyed them.

relationship: parallel plea for salvation revealing the only God to the kingdoms
rationale: Both ask God to rescue His people from Assyria so that the earth's kingdoms may know Him alone as God. The desired deliverance has the same expressly stated purpose.
source_text: But Thou, Lord our God, save us from their hand, so that every kingdom of the earth may know that Thou alone art God.”

target_units.text: Now, Lord our God, save us from his hand, and all the kingdoms of the earth will know that Thou art the Lord, God alone.’

relationship: parallel answer that Hezekiah's prayer was heard
rationale: Both introduce Isaiah's message to Hezekiah with God's declaration that He heard the prayer concerning Sennacherib king of the Assyrians.
source_text: Isaiah son of Amos was sent to Hezekiah and said to him, “Thus says the Lord, God of Israel: I heard what you prayed to Me about Sennacherib king of the Assyrians.

target_units.text: Isaiah son of Amos sent to Hezekiah: ‘Thus says the Lord, the God of hosts, Israel’s God: What you did pray to Me concerning Sennacherib king of the Assyrians, I have heard.

relationship: parallel personified Zion's derision of the Assyrian ruler
rationale: Both describe virgin daughter Zion despising and sneering at the ruler and daughter Jerusalem shaking her head over him. The matching female-city imagery conveys the same reversal of his intimidation.
source_text: This is the word God spoke concerning him: Virgin daughter Zion despised and sneered at you; daughter Jerusalem shook her head over you.

target_units.text: This is the word the Lord has spoken concerning him: Virgin daughter Zion despises you and sneers at you; daughter Jerusalem shakes her head at you.

relationship: parallel reproach challenge with different eye-language
rationale: Both ask whom the ruler reproached and against whom he raised his voice. Isaiah says he did not lift his eyes on high toward Israel's Holy One; Kings says he lifted them on high against Him. The different formulations are preserved.
source_text: Whom did you reproach and provoke? Against whom did you raise your voice? Yet you did not lift your eyes on high toward the Holy One of Israel.

target_units.text: Whom have you reproached and blasphemed? Against whom have you raised your voice? You have lifted your eyes on high against Israel’s Holy One!

relationship: parallel boast of chariots and cutting Lebanon's trees
rationale: Both recount reproach through messengers and a boast involving many chariots, mountain heights, Lebanon, cedars and cypresses. Isaiah describes the ascent as accomplished; Kings says the speaker shall climb, then describes cutting and arrival.
source_text: For through messengers you reproached the Lord. You said, ‘With my many chariots I climbed the mountain heights and the furthest reaches of Lebanon. I cut down its cedar’s height and the cypress’s beauty, and entered the height of a part of the woodland.

target_units.text: Through your messengers you did reproach the Lord and did say, “With the multitude of my chariots I shall climb the mountain heights, Lebanon’s flanks. I cut down its cedar’s height, its choice cypresses, and came to the melon of its farthest part, the woodland of its Carmel.

relationship: parallel boast of mastery over waters with differing actions
rationale: Both speeches boast of drying waters. Isaiah also says the speaker laid a bridge; Kings instead says he cooled and drank foreign waters and dried rivers with his foot's tread.
source_text: I laid a bridge and dried up waters and every gathering of water.’

target_units.text: I cooled and drank foreign waters, and with my foot’s tread I dried up all rivers of enclosure.”

relationship: parallel divine claim to have arranged the conquest
rationale: Isaiah attributes the devastation of fortified places to God's earlier arrangement; Kings likewise has God say He formed and brought about the outcome involving fortified cities and exiled fighting men. The formulations of the outcome differ.
source_text: Did you not hear long ago about these things I did? From ancient days I arranged them; now I have shown them: to desolate nations in strongholds and those dwelling in fortified cities.

target_units.text: I formed it; now I brought it. It became a carrying away into exiles of fighting men—fortified cities.

relationship: close weakened hands and rooftop-grass imagery
rationale: Isaiah joins hands let go with withering and grass on roofs; Kings describes inhabitants weak in hand and likens them to field grass and rooftop grass. The common imagery presents the conquered as unable to resist.
source_text: I let the hands go, and they withered and became like dry grass on roofs and like wild grass.

target_units.text: Their inhabitants grew weak in hand, cowered, and were ashamed. They became field grass or green herbage, rooftop grass, and a trampling before one standing.

relationship: parallel divine knowledge of the ruler's movements
rationale: Both declare God's knowledge of the ruler's rest or sitting, going out and coming in. Kings also includes his anger against God within this sentence.
source_text: But now I know your rest, your going out and your coming in.

target_units.text: I know your sitting, your going out, your coming in, and your anger against Me.

relationship: parallel restraint and return of the enraged Assyrian king
rationale: Both connect the ruler's anger rising to God with restraint at nose and lips and return along his incoming road. Isaiah names a muzzle in the nose; Kings names hooks in the nostrils, while both name a bridle in the lips.
source_text: Your wrath with which you raged, and your bitterness, have risen to Me. I will put a muzzle in your nose and a bridle in your lips, and turn you back by the way you came.

target_units.text: Because you were angry with Me and your arrogance rose to My ears, I shall put My hooks in your nostrils and a bridle in your lips, and turn you back by the road on which you came.

relationship: parallel three-year agricultural sign with different first-year wording
rationale: Both give a three-year sign culminating in sowing, reaping, planting vineyards and eating fruit. Isaiah's first year eats what has been sown; Kings instead specifies what grows by itself, followed by what sprouts in the second year.
source_text: This is your sign: This year eat what you have sown, in the second year what remains, and in the third, after sowing, reap and plant vineyards; you will eat their fruit.

target_units.text: This shall be the sign for you: You shall eat this year what grows by itself, and in the second year what sprouts. In the third, sowing, harvest, and planting vineyards; you shall eat their fruit.

relationship: parallel renewed growth of Judah's remnant
rationale: Both portray Judah's surviving remnant taking root below and producing above. Isaiah specifies seed above, while Kings specifies fruit upward.
source_text: Those remaining in Judea will grow a root below and produce seed above.

target_units.text: The rescued remnant of Judah’s house shall again take root downward and bear fruit upward.

relationship: parallel remnant emerging through the Lord's zeal
rationale: Both announce a remnant going out from Jerusalem and survivors from Mount Zion, concluding that the Lord's zeal will accomplish it.
source_text: For those remaining will go out from Jerusalem, and those being saved from Mount Zion. The zeal of the Lord Sabaoth will do these things.

target_units.text: For a remnant shall come out from Jerusalem, and one escaping from Mount Zion. The zeal of the Lord of hosts shall do this.

relationship: parallel denial of an Assyrian assault entering Jerusalem
rationale: Both deny the king entry into the city, the shooting of a missile or arrow, the bringing of a shield and the construction of siegeworks. The specified military actions closely correspond.
source_text: Therefore thus says the Lord against the king of the Assyrians: He will certainly not enter this city or shoot a missile against it; he will certainly not bring a shield against it or surround it with a siegework.

target_units.text: Not so! Thus says the Lord concerning the king of the Assyrians: He shall not enter this city or shoot an arrow there; no shield shall come before it, and he shall certainly not pour up a siege ramp against it.

relationship: parallel return by the same road
rationale: Both declare that Assyria's king will return by the road he came. Kings repeats the additional denial that he will enter the city.
source_text: By the way he came he will return. Thus says the Lord.

target_units.text: By the road on which he came he shall return; he shall not enter this city, says the Lord.

relationship: parallel divine shielding for God's and David's sake
rationale: Both promise that God will shield the city, giving God's own sake and David His servant as the stated reasons. Isaiah additionally explicitly says the shielding is to save it.
source_text: I will shield this city to save it, because of Me and because of David My servant.”

target_units.text: I shall shield this city for My own sake and for the sake of David My servant.’

relationship: parallel angelic destruction of 185000 Assyrians
rationale: Both record the Lord's angel striking one hundred eighty-five thousand in the Assyrian camp and the dead bodies found in the morning. Kings explicitly places the angel's action at night.
source_text: An angel of the Lord went out and killed one hundred eighty-five thousand from the Assyrians’ camp. On rising early in the morning, they found all the bodies dead.

target_units.text: By night the Lord’s angel went out and struck one hundred eighty-five thousand in the Assyrians’ camp. When they rose early in the morning, behold, they were all dead bodies.

relationship: parallel Assyrian withdrawal to Nineveh
rationale: Both record the Assyrian king departing and returning to live in Nineveh. Kings expressly names him Sennacherib in this sentence.
source_text: The king of the Assyrians turned back, went away, and lived in Nineveh.

target_units.text: Sennacherib king of the Assyrians departed, went away, returned, and lived in Nineveh.

relationship: parallel assassination by the king's sons during worship
rationale: Both name Adramelech and Sarasar striking their father with swords in his god's house, escaping, and Asordan succeeding him. Isaiah names the place of escape Armenia; Kings names Ararat, and the sanctuary's name also differs in form.
source_text: While he was worshiping his cult-image in the house of Nasarach, his sons Adramelech and Sarasar struck him with swords. They escaped safely to Armenia, and his son Asordan reigned in his place.

target_units.text: As he was bowing down in the house of Neserach his god, his sons Adramelech and Sarasar struck him with the sword and escaped to the land of Ararat. His son Asordan became king in his place.

relationship: parallel warning to the mortally ill Hezekiah
rationale: Both describe Hezekiah ill to the point of death and Isaiah son of Amos telling him to arrange his household because he is dying and will not live.
source_text: At that time Hezekiah became ill to the point of death. The prophet Isaiah son of Amos came to him and said, “Thus says the Lord: Arrange your household’s affairs, for you are dying and will not live.”

target_units.text: In those days Hezekiah became sick to the point of death. Isaiah son of Amos the prophet came to him and said, ‘Thus says the Lord: Give instructions for your house, for you are dying and shall not live.’

relationship: parallel prayer with face turned to the wall
rationale: Both record Hezekiah turning his face toward the wall and praying to the Lord after Isaiah's announcement concerning his illness.
source_text: Hezekiah turned his face toward the wall and prayed to the Lord,

target_units.text: Hezekiah turned his face to the wall and prayed to the Lord,

relationship: parallel appeal to faithful conduct followed by weeping
rationale: Both prayers ask God to remember Hezekiah's truthful walk, heart and conduct pleasing to Him, followed by his intense weeping. Isaiah calls the heart true; Kings calls it full.
source_text: saying, “Remember, Lord, how I walked before Thee with truth, in a true heart, and did what was pleasing before Thee.” Hezekiah wept greatly.

target_units.text: ‘I pray Thee, Lord, remember how I walked before Thee in truth and with a full heart, and did what was good in Thine eyes.’ Hezekiah wept bitterly.

relationship: parallel divine message to Isaiah after Hezekiah's prayer
rationale: Both place a new word from the Lord to Isaiah after Hezekiah's prayer and before the reassuring response. Kings adds Isaiah's location in the middle courtyard and the instruction to return to the king.
source_text: The Lord’s word came to Isaiah, saying,

target_units.text: Isaiah was in the middle courtyard when the Lord’s word came to him:

‘Return and tell Hezekiah, leader of My people: Thus says the Lord, the God of your father David: I have heard your prayer and seen your tears. Behold, I shall heal you; on the third day you shall go up to the Lord’s house,

relationship: parallel heard prayer and fifteen additional years
rationale: Both answers identify God as the God of David, say He heard the prayer and saw the tears, and promise Hezekiah fifteen further years. Kings additionally gives a third-day return to the Lord's house.
source_text: “Go and tell Hezekiah: Thus says the Lord, God of David your father: I heard the voice of your prayer and saw your tears. Behold, I am adding fifteen years to your time.

target_units.text: ‘Return and tell Hezekiah, leader of My people: Thus says the Lord, the God of your father David: I have heard your prayer and seen your tears. Behold, I shall heal you; on the third day you shall go up to the Lord’s house,
and I shall add fifteen years to your days. I shall save you and this city from the hand of the king of the Assyrians, and shield this city for My own sake and for the sake of David My servant.’

relationship: parallel promise to save Hezekiah and shield Jerusalem
rationale: Both promise rescue from the Assyrian king and shielding of the city. Kings additionally states God's own sake and David His servant as reasons.
source_text: I will save you from the king of the Assyrians’ hand, and I will shield this city.

target_units.text: and I shall add fifteen years to your days. I shall save you and this city from the hand of the king of the Assyrians, and shield this city for My own sake and for the sake of David My servant.’

relationship: parallel introduction of the confirming sign
rationale: Both introduce a sign from the Lord that He will carry out His announced word. Kings continues immediately with the shadow's steps, while Isaiah gives the sign's description in the following unit.
source_text: This is your sign from the Lord that God will do this thing:”

target_units.text: Isaiah said, ‘This is the sign from the Lord that the Lord will do the word He has spoken: The shadow will advance ten steps, if it returns ten steps.’

relationship: parallel ten-step reversal with sun and shadow distinguished
rationale: Isaiah describes the sun turned back the ten steps descended by the shadow; Kings records Hezekiah's request and Isaiah's prayer followed by the shadow returning ten steps. The stated subject of the reversal differs.
source_text: “As for the shadow of the steps the sun descended—the ten steps of your father’s house—I will turn the sun back ten steps.” The sun went up the ten steps which the shadow had descended.

target_units.text: Hezekiah said, ‘It is easy for the shadow to incline ten steps. No, let the shadow return ten steps backward.’
Isaiah the prophet cried to the Lord, and the shadow returned backward ten steps on the stairway.

relationship: parallel identification of Hezekiah's prayer during mortal illness
rationale: Isaiah identifies the ensuing prayer with Hezekiah's illness and recovery; Chronicles likewise names his illness to the point of death, prayer, God's hearing and a sign. Chronicles does not reproduce the prayer's words.
source_text: A prayer of Hezekiah king of Judea, when he became ill and rose from his illness:

target_units.text: In those days Hezekiah became ill to the point of death. He prayed to the Lord, and He listened to him and gave him a sign.

relationship: related gates-of-death imagery within prayer for life
rationale: Hezekiah recalls reaching Hades' gates at the height of his days; the psalm addresses God as raising the speaker from death's gates so that he may proclaim praise. The endangered life and subsequent praise connect the prayers.
source_text: I said, “At the height of my days, at Hades’ gates, I will leave my remaining years behind.”

target_units.text: Have mercy on me, Lord; see my humiliation from my enemies, Thou who raisest me from the gates of death,
so that I may proclaim all Thy praises in the gates of daughter Zion; I will exult in Thy salvation.

relationship: contrast between feared loss and hoped-for sight of God's good
rationale: Hezekiah recalls expecting no longer to see God's salvation upon earth; the psalmist believes he will see the Lord's good things in the land of the living. Both frame continued earthly life through seeing divine good, with opposite stated expectations.
source_text: I said, “I will certainly no longer see God’s salvation upon the earth; I will certainly no longer see a person

target_units.text: I believe that I will see the Lord’s good things in the land of the living.

relationship: shared mortal-life image of a dismantled tent
rationale: Hezekiah likens his departing life to taking down a pitched tent; Paul describes the earthly tent being dismantled and contrasts it with an eternal dwelling from God. Isaiah's additional weaver-web image is not repeated in the target.
source_text: from my family. I left the rest of my life; it went out and departed from me like someone taking down a tent he had pitched. My spirit beside me became like a weaver’s web as she approached to cut it off. On that day I was handed over

target_units.text: For we know that if our earthly house, this tent, is dismantled, we have a building from God, a house not made by hands, eternal in the heavens.
For indeed in this we groan, longing to be clothed over with our dwelling from heaven,
if indeed, even after being unclothed, we shall not be found naked.
For indeed we who are in the tent groan, being burdened, because we do not wish to be unclothed but to be clothed over, so that what is mortal may be swallowed up by life.

relationship: related crushing affliction described with bones and a lion
rationale: Hezekiah describes being handed over as to a lion and his bones crushed; Lamentations describes shattered bones and the afflicter as a lion in hiding. The two laments combine bodily breaking and a predatory image.
source_text: until morning, as to a lion; thus he crushed my bones, for from day to night I was handed over.

target_units.text: He made my flesh and my skin old; He shattered my bones.
He built against me, surrounded my head and toiled.
He made me dwell in dark places like the dead of ages.
He built against me, and I will not go out; He made my bronze heavy.
Indeed, I will cry and call out; He blocked my prayer.
He built up my roads, blocked my paths and troubled them.
He is a bear lying in wait for me, a lion in hidden places.

relationship: close crying and eyes failing while looking toward God
rationale: Hezekiah speaks of crying and says his eyes failed from looking heavenward toward the Lord; the psalmist is weary from crying and says his eyes failed from hoping in God. The psalm does not repeat the swallow and dove comparisons.
source_text: Like a swallow I will cry out, and like a dove I will murmur. For my eyes failed from looking toward heaven’s height, toward the Lord who rescued me

target_units.text: I grew weary crying out; my throat became hoarse; my eyes failed from hoping in my God.

relationship: parallel relief of the soul's mortal distress
rationale: Hezekiah says the Lord took away his soul's pain; the psalm moves from death's pangs, affliction and pain to the soul's rest and rescue from death. Both give the Lord credit for that relief.
source_text: and took away my soul’s pain.

target_units.text: The pangs of death surrounded me; the dangers of Hades found me; I found affliction and pain.
And I called on the name of the Lord: “O Lord, rescue my soul!”
Merciful is the Lord, and righteous; and our God shows mercy.
The Lord guards the little children; I was humbled, and He saved me.
Return, my soul, to your rest, for the Lord has benefited you,
for He rescued my soul from death, my eyes from tears, and my feet from slipping.

relationship: parallel divine restoration from threatened death
rationale: Hezekiah addresses the Lord who raised his breath so that he lived comforted; the psalmist thanks God for healing him and bringing his soul up from Hades. The supplied expressions of restored life differ.
source_text: For, Lord, a report about it was brought to Thee, and Thou didst raise my breath; comforted, I lived.

target_units.text: Lord my God, I cried out unto Thee, and Thou didst heal me.
Lord, Thou broughtest my soul up from Hades; Thou didst save me from those descending into a pit.

relationship: parallel removal of sins through spatial casting imagery
rationale: Hezekiah says God cast his sins behind him; Micah describes sins thrown into the sea's depths after divine mercy. The positions differ, and Isaiah's wording is behind the speaker, not behind God's back.
source_text: For Thou didst choose my soul so that it would not perish, and didst cast all my sins behind me.

target_units.text: Who is a God like Thee, removing injustices and passing over impieties for the remaining ones of His inheritance? He did not retain His anger as a testimony, because He desires mercy.
He Himself will turn back and pity us; He will sink our injustices, and they will be thrown into the depths of the sea—all our sins.

relationship: close denial of praise from death and Hades
rationale: Hezekiah says those in Hades will not praise or hope for God's mercy; the psalm likewise says no one in death remembers God and asks who gives Him thanks in Hades.
source_text: For those in Hades will not praise Thee, nor will the dead bless Thee, nor will those in Hades hope for Thy mercy.

target_units.text: For in death there is no one who remembers Thee; and in Hades, who will give Thee thanks?

relationship: related future children announcing God's deeds
rationale: Hezekiah anticipates children who will announce God's righteousness; the psalm describes another generation and sons yet to be born learning and announcing God's praises and works to their sons. Both extend divine acknowledgment to future offspring.
source_text: The living will bless Thee, as I do. For from today I will have children who will announce Thy righteousness,

target_units.text: it was not hidden from their children for another generation, as we announce the Lord’s praises, His mighty acts and the wonders He did.
And He raised a testimony in Jacob and set a law in Israel, whatever He commanded our fathers to make known to their sons,
so that another generation might know, sons who will be born; and they will rise and announce it to their sons,
so that they may set their hope upon God and not forget God’s works, and seek out His commandments,

relationship: parallel lifelong worship associated with God's house
rationale: Hezekiah promises harp-blessing throughout his life before God's house; the psalm seeks residence in the Lord's house all life's days and promises song and music in its worship. The particular instrument is specified only in Isaiah.
source_text: Lord of my salvation. I will not cease blessing Thee with a harp all the days of my life before God’s house.”

target_units.text: One thing I asked from the Lord; this I will seek: that I may dwell in the Lord’s house all the days of my life, that I may behold the Lord’s loveliness and visit His temple.
For He hid me in a tent in the day of my troubles; He sheltered me in the hiding place of His tent; He raised me upon a rock.
And now, behold, He raised my head above my enemies; I went around and sacrificed in His tent a sacrifice of shouting; I will sing and make music to the Lord.

relationship: parallel medicinal application of a fig cake
rationale: Both describe a cake of figs applied for Hezekiah's recovery. Isaiah specifies crushing it into a poultice; Kings expressly names the ulcer to which it is placed.
source_text: Isaiah said to Hezekiah, “Take a cake made of figs, crush it and apply it as a poultice, and you will be healthy.”

target_units.text: He said, ‘Let them take a cake of figs and place it on the ulcer, and he will recover.’

relationship: parallel Hezekiah sign statement concerning the Lord's house
rationale: Both connect Hezekiah's sign with going up to the Lord's house. Isaiah presents his words as a declaration, while Kings presents a question and specifies healing and the third day.
source_text: Hezekiah said, “This is the sign that I will go up to the house of the Lord God.”

target_units.text: Hezekiah said to Isaiah, ‘What is the sign that the Lord will heal me and I shall go up to the Lord’s house on the third day?’

relationship: parallel Babylonian correspondence after Hezekiah's illness
rationale: Both name Babylon's king sending letters after hearing of Hezekiah's illness. Isaiah names gifts, envoys and his recovery; Kings calls the accompanying items manaa, and the royal name forms differ.
source_text: At that time Marodach son of Laadan, king of Babylonia, sent letters, envoys, and gifts to Hezekiah, for he heard that he had been ill to the point of death and had recovered.

target_units.text: At that time Marodachbaladan son of Baladan, king of Babylon, sent letters and manaa to Hezekiah, because he heard that Hezekiah was sick.

relationship: parallel delighted display of Hezekiah's treasures
rationale: Both describe Hezekiah rejoicing over the visitors and showing his stores of silver, gold, fragrant substances and equipment, withholding none of his household treasures. The inventories differ in their particular terms.
source_text: Hezekiah rejoiced greatly over them and showed them the store of nekhotha, liquid myrrh, incense, perfumed ointment, silver, gold, all the storerooms of the treasury’s equipment, and everything in his treasuries. There was nothing in his house that Hezekiah did not show.

target_units.text: Hezekiah rejoiced over them and showed them the whole house of the nechotha: the silver, gold, spices, fine oil, the house of equipment, and everything found in his treasuries. There was nothing in his house or all his authority that Hezekiah did not show them.

relationship: parallel Isaiah's question about the visitors' origin
rationale: Both have Isaiah ask Hezekiah what the visitors said and where they came from, followed by Hezekiah's answer that they came from the distant land of Babylon.
source_text: The prophet Isaiah came to King Hezekiah and said, “What are these men saying, and from where have they come to you?” Hezekiah said, “They have come to me from a distant land, from Babylon.”

target_units.text: Isaiah the prophet came to King Hezekiah and said, ‘What did these men say, and from where have they come to you?’ Hezekiah said, ‘They have come to me from a distant land, from Babylon.’

relationship: parallel admission that all the treasures were shown
rationale: Both record Isaiah asking what the visitors saw and Hezekiah admitting that they saw everything in his house, including the treasuries, without anything withheld.
source_text: Isaiah said, “What did they see in your house?” Hezekiah said, “They saw everything in my house. There is nothing in my house they did not see, and also the things in my treasuries.”

target_units.text: He said, ‘What have they seen in your house?’ He said, ‘They saw everything in my house. There was nothing in my house that I did not show them, and also the things in my treasuries.’

relationship: parallel introduction of the Babylonian exile warning
rationale: Both place Isaiah's instruction to hear the Lord's word immediately before the prediction that Hezekiah's ancestral stores will be taken to Babylon. The introduction belongs to the same identified encounter.
source_text: Isaiah said to him, “Hear the word of the Lord Sabaoth:

target_units.text: Isaiah said to Hezekiah, ‘Hear the Lord’s word:

relationship: parallel prediction of ancestral treasures taken to Babylon
rationale: Both predict that everything in Hezekiah's house and accumulated by his fathers will be taken to Babylon. Isaiah says nothing will be left; Kings' concluding clause says no word spoken by the Lord will be left over.
source_text: Behold, days are coming, says the Lord, and they will take everything in your house. What your fathers gathered until this day will reach Babylon, and they will certainly leave nothing behind. God also said

target_units.text: Behold, days are coming when everything in your house, and what your fathers stored up to this day, shall be taken to Babylon. No word which the Lord spoke shall be left over.

relationship: parallel prediction of royal descendants serving as eunuchs
rationale: Both predict that Hezekiah's offspring will be taken and made eunuchs in the Babylonian king's house. The relationship concerns the expressly stated descendants, destination and service.
source_text: that they will also take some of your children whom you fathered and make them eunuchs in the house of the Babylonians’ king.”

target_units.text: He shall take your sons who come forth from you, whom you beget, and they shall be eunuchs in the house of the king of Babylon.’

relationship: related royal descendants brought into Babylonian service
rationale: Isaiah predicts royal offspring taken into Babylon's king's house; Daniel records the king's order for young men from Israel's royal family to be educated for his service. Daniel puts them under a chief eunuch but does not expressly state that the young men were made eunuchs.
source_text: that they will also take some of your children whom you fathered and make them eunuchs in the house of the Babylonians’ king.”

target_units.text: The king told Abiesdri, his chief eunuch, to bring him some of the sons of Israel’s magnates, of the royal family and of the chosen men:

young men without blemish, handsome, knowledgeable in every kind of wisdom, literate, intelligent, wise, and strong enough to be in the king’s house, and to teach them letters and the Chaldean tongue,
and to give them a ration from the king’s house each day, from the royal table and the wine the king drank, and to educate them for three years and place some of them before the king.

relationship: parallel acceptance of the warning and wish for peace
rationale: Both record Hezekiah calling the Lord's word good and asking for peace in his own days. Isaiah additionally includes righteousness in that wish.
source_text: Hezekiah said to Isaiah, “The Lord’s word that He spoke is good. Let there indeed be peace and righteousness in my days.”

target_units.text: Hezekiah said to Isaiah, ‘The word of the Lord which He spoke is good. Let there be peace in my days.’

relationship: internal promise of comfort for God's people and Zion
rationale: God's command to comfort His people is developed in the later promise to comfort Zion and her deserted places, with joy, thanksgiving and praise. Both concern comfort of the community addressed by God.
source_text: Comfort, comfort My people, says God.

target_units.text: I will now comfort you, Zion; I have comforted all her deserted places and will make her deserted places like the Lord’s paradise. They will find joy and exultation in her, thanksgiving and a voice of praise.

relationship: related announcement of release for Jerusalem and Zion
rationale: Isaiah comforts Jerusalem because humiliation is fulfilled and sin loosed; Lamentations likewise tells daughter Zion that her lawlessness has ended and she will be deported no longer. The formulations of the release differ.
source_text: You priests, speak to the heart of Jerusalem; comfort her. For her humiliation is fulfilled, her sin is loosed; for from the hand of the Lord she has received double for her sins.

target_units.text: Your lawlessness has ended, Daughter Zion; He will deport you no longer. He has visited your acts of lawlessness, Daughter Edom; He has uncovered your acts of ungodliness.

relationship: close double repayment for sins
rationale: Isaiah says Jerusalem received double for her sins from the Lord's hand; Jeremiah likewise announces double repayment for injustices and sins. Isaiah looks back in a message of comfort, while Jeremiah announces the penalty.
source_text: You priests, speak to the heart of Jerusalem; comfort her. For her humiliation is fulfilled, her sin is loosed; for from the hand of the Lord she has received double for her sins.

target_units.text: And I will repay double their injustices and sins, for which they profaned My land with the corpses of their abominations and with their lawless acts, by which they offended against My inheritance.

relationship: explicit quotation identifying the wilderness voice
rationale: Luke names the book of Isaiah and quotes the wilderness voice calling for the Lord's way to be prepared and His paths straightened, within its account of John's preaching.
source_text: A voice of one crying in the wilderness: Prepare the way of the Lord; make straight the paths of our God.

target_units.text: as it is written in the book of the words of Isaiah the prophet: “A voice of one crying in the wilderness: Prepare the Lord’s way; make His paths straight.

relationship: explicit use of Isaiah's voice saying as John's self-description
rationale: Asked who he is, John identifies himself as the wilderness voice and cites Isaiah's instruction to straighten the Lord's way. This is an expressly attributed use of the source's distinctive wording.
source_text: A voice of one crying in the wilderness: Prepare the way of the Lord; make straight the paths of our God.

target_units.text: So they said to him, “Who are you, so that we may give an answer to those who sent us? What do you say about yourself?”
He said, “I am a voice of one crying in the wilderness, ‘Make straight the way of the Lord,’ just as Isaiah the prophet said.”

relationship: explicit application of the wilderness voice to John the Baptist
rationale: Matthew introduces John's wilderness proclamation and says he is the one spoken of through Isaiah, then quotes the command to prepare the Lord's way and straighten His paths.
source_text: A voice of one crying in the wilderness: Prepare the way of the Lord; make straight the paths of our God.

target_units.text: In those days John the Baptist appeared, proclaiming in the wilderness of Judea
and saying, “Repent, for the kingdom of the heavens has drawn near.”
For this is the one spoken of through Isaiah the prophet: “A voice of one crying in the wilderness: ‘Prepare the way of the Lord; make His paths straight.’”

relationship: explicit wilderness-voice citation introducing John's ministry
rationale: Mark includes the wilderness voice and preparation of the Lord's way in the citation introduced under Isaiah's name, immediately before John's appearance. Its preceding messenger clause is additional to the wording of this Isaiah unit.
source_text: A voice of one crying in the wilderness: Prepare the way of the Lord; make straight the paths of our God.

target_units.text: As it is written in Isaiah the prophet: “Look, I send My messenger before Thy face, who will prepare Thy way;
a voice of one crying in the wilderness, ‘Prepare the way of the Lord; make His paths straight.’”
John appeared, baptizing in the wilderness and proclaiming a baptism of repentance for the forgiveness of sins.

relationship: explicit quotation of transformed terrain
rationale: Luke's Isaiah quotation repeats valleys or ravines filled, mountains and hills lowered, crooked places straightened and rough ways made smooth. These concrete changes correspond to the source's preparation of the way.
source_text: Every valley will be filled, and every mountain and hill will be brought low; all the crooked places will become straight, and the rough country will become plains.

target_units.text: Every ravine will be filled, and every mountain and hill brought low. The crooked will become straight, and the rough ways smooth roads,

relationship: explicit quotation of all flesh seeing God's salvation
rationale: Luke concludes its cited Isaiah passage with all flesh seeing God's salvation. Isaiah additionally says the Lord's glory will be seen and grounds the promise in His spoken word.
source_text: And the glory of the Lord will be seen, and all flesh will see the salvation of God; for the Lord has spoken.

target_units.text: and all flesh will see God’s salvation.”

relationship: internal promise of God's salvation seen universally
rationale: Both announce the sight of God's salvation beyond a single community: all flesh here and all earth's ends in Isaiah 52, where God's holy arm is revealed before the nations.
source_text: And the glory of the Lord will be seen, and all flesh will see the salvation of God; for the Lord has spoken.

target_units.text: The Lord will uncover His holy arm before all nations, and all the ends of earth will see the salvation that comes from God.

relationship: quotation of human flesh and glory as grass and flower
rationale: First Peter repeats the comparison of all flesh with grass and its glory with the grass's flower. Its surrounding argument contrasts perishable life with rebirth through God's enduring word.
source_text: A voice says, “Cry out!” And I said, “What shall I cry?” All flesh is grass, and all the glory of man is as the flower of grass.

target_units.text: For “All flesh is like grass, and all its glory like a flower of grass. The grass withered, and the flower fell,

relationship: quotation of withered grass and fallen flower
rationale: First Peter repeats the source's paired statements that the grass withered and the flower fell, within the same comparison between mortal humanity and God's enduring word.
source_text: The grass has withered, and the flower has fallen;

target_units.text: For “All flesh is like grass, and all its glory like a flower of grass. The grass withered, and the flower fell,

relationship: quotation of the perpetually enduring divine word
rationale: First Peter repeats that the Lord's word remains forever and identifies it with the good news proclaimed to its hearers. Isaiah names it the word of our God.
source_text: but the word of our God remains for ever.

target_units.text: but the word of the Lord remains forever.” And this is the word that was proclaimed to you as good news.

relationship: related permanence of divine and Jesus' words
rationale: Isaiah declares God's word enduring forever; Jesus declares that His words will not pass away even though heaven and earth will. The sayings share enduring speech while naming their speakers differently.
source_text: but the word of our God remains for ever.

target_units.text: Heaven and earth will pass away, but My words will certainly not pass away.

relationship: internal mountain-borne good news concerning Zion's God
rationale: Both join mountains, good news addressed to Zion and proclamation concerning her God. Isaiah 40 says to announce 'Behold your God' to Judah's cities; Isaiah 52 announces peace, salvation and God's reign.
source_text: Go up on a high mountain, you who bring good news to Zion; lift up your voice with strength, you who bring good news to Jerusalem. Lift up; do not fear. Say to the cities of Judah, Behold your God!

target_units.text: like beauty on the mountains, like the feet of one proclaiming a report of peace, like one bringing good news. For I will make your salvation heard, saying, ‘Zion, your God will reign.’”

relationship: close arrival with reward and work before the arriving Savior
rationale: Both announce an arrival with reward and work before Him. Isaiah 40 describes the Lord coming with might and dominion; Isaiah 62 tells daughter Zion that her Savior is arriving.
source_text: Behold, the Lord comes with might, and His arm with dominion; behold, His reward is with Him, and His work before Him.

target_units.text: For behold, the Lord has made it heard to earth’s farthest end: “Tell daughter Zion, ‘Behold, the savior is arriving for you, bringing His own reward and His work before His face.’”

relationship: parallel divine shepherding and care of vulnerable sheep
rationale: Isaiah portrays God shepherding, gathering lambs and comforting those with young; Ezekiel likewise promises God's personal gathering, feeding and care of lost, broken and failing sheep. The particular vulnerable groups differ.
source_text: Like a shepherd, He will shepherd His flock; and with His arm He will gather lambs, and comfort those that are with young.

target_units.text: For thus says the Lord: Behold, I will seek out My sheep and visit them.

As a shepherd seeks his flock on a day when there is gloom and cloud among separated sheep, so I will seek out My sheep and drive them away from every place where they scattered on a day of cloud and gloom.

I will bring them out from the nations, gather them from the countries and bring them into their own land. I will feed them upon Israel’s mountains, in the ravines and in every dwelling place of the land.
I will feed them in good pasture, and their folds will be upon Israel’s high mountain. There they will lie down, there rest in good delight, and graze in rich pasture upon Israel’s mountains.
I Myself will feed My sheep and give them rest, and they will know that I am the Lord. Thus says the Lord, the Lord:
I will seek the lost, bring back the wandering, bind up the broken, strengthen the failing and guard the strong. I will feed them with judgment.

relationship: related questions about cosmic mastery through physical images
rationale: Isaiah asks who measures waters, heaven and earth and weighs mountains; Proverbs asks who wraps waters, gathers winds and takes hold of earth's ends. Both use bodily or household images to ask about mastery of creation, with different specific images.
source_text: Who measured the water with His hand, heaven with a span, and all the earth with a handful? Who weighed mountains with a weight and wooded valleys with a balance?

target_units.text: Who went up to heaven and came down? Who gathered winds in a fold of his garment? Who wrapped water in a cloak? Who took hold of all the ends of the earth? What is his name, or what is his children’s name, so that you may know?

relationship: explicit reuse of the Lord's mind and counselor questions
rationale: Romans repeats the questions about who knew the Lord's mind or became His counselor within praise of God's unsearchable wisdom and judgments.
source_text: Who knew the Lord’s mind, and who became His counselor to instruct Him?

target_units.text: “For who knew the Lord’s mind? Or who became His counselor?

relationship: quotation of knowing and instructing the Lord's mind
rationale: First Corinthians repeats the question about knowing the Lord's mind so as to instruct Him, then says that its speakers have Christ's mind. The surrounding explanation locates revealed knowledge in God's Spirit.
source_text: Who knew the Lord’s mind, and who became His counselor to instruct Him?

target_units.text: For “Who has known the Lord’s mind, so as to instruct Him?” But we have Christ’s mind.

relationship: complementary presentation of God as the source of understanding
rationale: Isaiah asks who instructed God or showed Him understanding; Job asks whether the Lord Himself teaches understanding and knowledge. The question about God's instructor is complemented by the affirmation that God teaches.
source_text: With whom did He take counsel, and who instructed Him? Who showed Him judgment, or who showed Him the way of understanding?

target_units.text: Is it not the Lord who teaches understanding and knowledge? He Himself will judge murders.

relationship: close drop-and-scales comparison of creation before God
rationale: Isaiah compares the nations with a bucket's drop and a scale's slight tipping; Wisdom compares the whole world before God with slight tipping of scales and a drop of morning dew. The scope and source of the drop differ.
source_text: If all the nations were counted like a drop from a bucket and like a scale’s slight tipping, they will also be counted like spittle.

target_units.text: For the whole world before Thee is like a slight tipping of the scales, and like a drop of morning dew that has fallen upon the earth.

relationship: related insufficiency of extravagant sacrificial provision
rationale: Isaiah says even Lebanon and all the four-footed animals are insufficient for a burnt offering; Micah asks whether thousands of rams and vast rich offerings secure approach to God, then names justice, mercy and walking with Him.
source_text: Lebanon is not sufficient for burning, nor all the four-footed animals sufficient for a whole burnt offering,

target_units.text: With what shall I take hold of the Lord and grasp my God Most High? Shall I take hold of Him with whole burnt offerings, with year-old calves?
Will the Lord receive with thousands of rams or with ten thousands of fat-rich torrents? Shall I give my firstborn offspring for impieties, the fruit of my body for the sin of my life?
Has it been declared to you, O man, what is good? Or what does the Lord seek from you, except to do justice, and to love mercy, and to be ready to walk with the Lord your God?

relationship: parallel human existence counted as nothing before God
rationale: Isaiah says all nations are counted as nothing; the psalmist calls his own existence nothing before God and extends vanity to every living person. The national and individual scopes differ.
source_text: and all the nations are as nothing and were counted as nothing.

target_units.text: Behold, Thou madest my days handbreadths, and my existence is as nothing before Thee. Yet all things are vanity—every living person. Diapsalma.

relationship: parallel question of God's incomparability
rationale: Isaiah asks to whom the Lord has been likened; the song in Exodus asks who is like the Lord among gods and praises His glory and wonders. Exodus answers through praise rather than Isaiah's following discussion of images.
source_text: To whom did you liken the Lord, and to what likeness did you liken Him?

target_units.text: Who is like Thee among the gods, O Lord? Who is like Thee, glorified among the holy ones, marvellous in glories, working wonders?

relationship: close human manufacture and gilding of an image
rationale: Isaiah questions a craftsman's image and a goldsmith's melted and applied gold; Jeremiah likewise describes applied silver, gold and the goldsmiths' hands as artisans' works. Jeremiah additionally describes the images' colored clothing.
source_text: Did a craftsman make an image, or did a goldsmith melt gold and gild it, fashioning it as a likeness?

target_units.text: It is worked silver; they will not walk. Applied silver will come from Tarshish, gold from Mophaz, and the goldsmiths’ hand; all are artisans’ works. They will dress them in blue and purple.

relationship: close wooden image secured against movement
rationale: Both describe a crafted wooden image set so it will not move or shake. Isaiah emphasizes selecting wood that will not rot; Jeremiah specifies metal adornment and fastening with hammers and nails.
source_text: For a craftsman chooses wood that will not rot and skillfully seeks how to set up his image so that it will not shake.

target_units.text: For the nations’ customs are futile: it is wood cut from the woodland, a carpenter’s work and a cast object.
They are adorned with silver and gold; with hammers and nails they fastened them, and they will not move.

relationship: parallel questions about knowledge of earth's foundations
rationale: Isaiah asks whether the hearers knew earth's foundations; the Lord asks Job where he was when those foundations were laid and whether he understands their measures and support. The addressees and rhetorical situations differ.
source_text: Will you not know? Will you not hear? Was it not announced to you from the beginning? Did you not know the earth’s foundations?

target_units.text: Where were you when I laid the earth’s foundation? Report to Me, if you understand.
Who set its measures, if you know? Or who brought a cord upon it?
Upon what have its rings been fixed, and who placed a cornerstone upon it,

relationship: close heaven stretched as a fabric dwelling or covering
rationale: Isaiah describes God stretching heaven like a tent to inhabit; the psalm describes Him stretching heaven like a hide curtain. The shared extended-covering image concerns God's making of heaven.
source_text: He holds the earth’s circuit, and its inhabitants are like locusts. He set heaven like a vault and stretched it out like a tent to dwell in.

target_units.text: wrapping Thyself in light like a garment, stretching out heaven like a hide curtain;

relationship: historical illustration of God removing a ruler's authority
rationale: Isaiah says God gives rulers nothing to rule; Daniel's heavenly announcement takes Nebuchadnezzar's kingdom and authority from him and gives them to another. This illustrates the rulership clause, not Isaiah's additional description of earth as nothing.
source_text: He gives rulers nothing to rule and made the earth as nothing.

target_units.text: At the completion of his word, he heard a voice from heaven: “To you it is said, King Nebuchadnezzar: Babylon’s kingdom has been taken from you and is given to another, a despised man in your house. Behold! I appoint him over your kingdom; he will take your authority, glory, and luxury, so that you may recognize that the God of heaven has authority over human kingship and will give it to whomever He wishes. By sunrise another king will rejoice in your house and take possession of your glory, strength, and authority.

relationship: related plant-and-wind contrast for insecure human life
rationale: Isaiah describes roots failing to establish, drying under God's breath and storm-driven brushwood; the psalm contrasts a rooted fruitful tree with ungodly people like wind-flung chaff. The plant materials and stated causes differ.
source_text: For they will certainly not sow or plant, nor will their root take hold in the earth. He blew on them, and they dried; a storm will carry them away like brushwood.

target_units.text: He will be like the tree planted beside the outlets of waters, which will give its fruit in its season, and whose leaf will not fall off; and everything he does will be prospered.
Not so the ungodly, not so, but like chaff which the wind flings away from the face of the earth.

relationship: parallel denial of any likeness to God
rationale: The Holy One asks to whom He has been likened; the psalm declares that no god is like the Lord and nothing is like His works and that He alone is the great God. Both make the comparison fail.
source_text: “Now then, to whom did you liken Me, and shall I be exalted?” said the Holy One.

target_units.text: There is none like Thee among gods, Lord, and nothing is like Thy works.
All the nations Thou madest will come and bow down before Thee, Lord, and glorify Thy name,
for Thou art great and dost wondrous things; Thou alone art the great God.

relationship: close divine numbering and naming of the heavenly array
rationale: Isaiah describes God bringing out His array by number and calling all by name; the psalm expressly names the multitude of stars that He numbers and calls by names. Both join this with His great strength.
source_text: Lift your eyes on high and see: Who displayed all these? He brings out His array by number and will call all by name. From abundant glory and in strength’s might, nothing escaped you.

target_units.text: He numbers multitudes of stars and calls them all by names.
Great is our Lord, and great is His strength; His understanding is beyond number.

relationship: internal challenge to a complaint of divine abandonment
rationale: Jacob and Israel say their way is hidden and their God removed judgment and departed; Zion later says the Lord abandoned and forgot her, and receives His denial of forgetting. Both settings answer the community's perception of neglect.
source_text: Do not say, Jacob—and why did you declare, Israel—“My way was hidden from God, and my God removed judgment and departed”?

target_units.text: But Zion said, “The Lord has abandoned me, and the Lord has forgotten me.”
“Will a woman forget her child, failing to have mercy on the offspring of her belly? Even if a woman forgets these, I will not forget you,” said the Lord.
“Behold, on My hands I painted your walls, and you are before Me continually.

relationship: parallel greatness and unsearchable understanding of God
rationale: Isaiah names the eternal Creator whose understanding cannot be discovered; the psalm likewise declares His great strength and understanding beyond number. The psalm does not repeat Isaiah's statements about hunger and weariness.
source_text: And now, did you not know, if you have not heard? God is eternal, the God who fashioned the earth’s extremities. He will not hunger or grow weary, and His understanding cannot be discovered.

target_units.text: Great is our Lord, and great is His strength; His understanding is beyond number.

relationship: related divine provision for hungry people
rationale: Isaiah says God gives strength to the hungry; the psalm says He gives them food. The correspondence concerns God's aid to the hungry, without equating strength and food as identical wording.
source_text: He gives strength to the hungry, and grief to those who are not in pain.

target_units.text: who does justice for those wronged, who gives food to the hungry. The Lord releases those in fetters.

relationship: related reversal from present ease to grief
rationale: Isaiah also says God gives grief to those not in pain; Jesus warns the rich who have received consolation and those laughing now that mourning and weeping will follow. This comparison addresses the source's second clause rather than replacing it with a familiar weakness saying.
source_text: He gives strength to the hungry, and grief to those who are not in pain.

target_units.text: But woe to you who are rich, because you have received your consolation.
Woe to you who are filled now, because you will hunger. Woe to you who laugh now, because you will mourn and weep.

relationship: related limits of human strength beside divine sustaining help
rationale: Isaiah describes younger and chosen men becoming hungry, weary and without strength; the psalm denies rescue through a giant's strength or military force and attributes rescue and nourishment in famine to God. The named human groups differ.
source_text: For younger people will hunger, young men will grow weary, and chosen men will be without strength.

target_units.text: A king is not saved through a great force, and a giant will not be saved by the abundance of his strength.
A horse is false for salvation, and by the abundance of its power it will not be saved.
Behold, the Lord’s eyes are upon those who fear Him, those who hope in His mercy,
to rescue their souls from death and nourish them in famine.

relationship: close renewed strength or youth associated with an eagle
rationale: Isaiah promises those enduring for God exchanged strength and wings like eagles; the psalm promises youth renewed like an eagle's after God's filling with good things. The images differ between growing wings and renewed youth.
source_text: But those enduring for God will exchange their strength and grow wings like eagles. They will run without growing weary and walk without hunger.

target_units.text: who fills your desire with good things; your youth will be renewed like an eagle’s.

relationship: internal summons of nations and rulers to a judicial encounter
rationale: Isaiah 41 summons islands and rulers to approach, speak and announce judgment; Isaiah 43 gathers nations and rulers and asks for witnesses and true statements. Both frame the challenge through public announcement and judgment.
source_text: “Be renewed toward Me, islands, for rulers will exchange their strength. Let them approach and speak together; then let them announce judgment.

target_units.text: All nations were gathered together, and rulers from them will assemble. Who will announce these things, or who will announce to you the things from the beginning? Let them bring their witnesses, be justified, and speak true things.

relationship: related divine rousing associated with righteousness
rationale: Isaiah 41 describes righteousness roused from the east and called to God's feet, using feminine pronouns; Isaiah 45 describes God raising a king with righteousness and directing his ways. The feminine figure is not replaced by that king's identity.
source_text: Who roused righteousness from the east, called her to His feet, and she will go? He will set her before nations, astonish kings, and put their swords into the earth and their bows like brushwood driven away.

target_units.text: I raised him as king with righteousness, and all his ways are straight. He will rebuild My city and bring back My people’s captivity, without ransom or gifts,” said the Lord Sabaoth.

relationship: internal affirmation of God's priority and continuing existence
rationale: Isaiah 41 identifies God as first and present for what is coming; Isaiah 44 declares Him first and after these things, with no God apart from Him. The formulations affirm His unmatched continuity without importing a different title.
source_text: Who acted and did these things? He called her, the One calling her from the generations’ beginning: I, God, am first, and for the things coming I am.

target_units.text: Thus says God, Israel’s King, who rescued him, God Sabaoth: “I am first, and I am after these things; apart from Me there is no God.

relationship: parallel gathering of rulers or nations marked by fear
rationale: Isaiah describes nations seeing and fearing and earth's extremities drawing together; the psalm describes gathered kings seeing, marveling and being shaken with trembling. The scenes share sight, assembly and fear before divine power.
source_text: Nations saw and feared; the earth’s extremities drew near and came together,

target_units.text: For behold, the kings gathered; they came together.
They saw and thus marveled; they were troubled and shaken.
Trembling seized them; there were pangs like a woman giving birth.

relationship: close crafted images fastened with nails so they will not move
rationale: Isaiah describes craftsmen's hammering, joining and strengthening the objects with nails; Jeremiah likewise names human craftsmanship and fastening with hammers and nails so that the objects will not move.
source_text: ‘A craftsman grew strong, and a smith striking with a hammer while also beating out the work.’ At one time he will say, ‘The joining is good.’ They strengthened them with nails; they will set them in place, and they will not move.

target_units.text: For the nations’ customs are futile: it is wood cut from the woodland, a carpenter’s work and a cast object.
They are adorned with silver and gold; with hammers and nails they fastened them, and they will not move.

relationship: related divine affection and friendship associated with Abraham
rationale: Isaiah identifies Abraham as the one God loved; James names him a friend of God after recounting his belief reckoned as righteousness. The descriptions correspond without substituting 'friend' for Isaiah's actual wording.
source_text: But you, Israel, My servant Jacob whom I chose, offspring of Abraham whom I loved,

target_units.text: and the Scripture was fulfilled that says, “Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness,” and he was called a friend of God.

relationship: parallel Israel's divine choice and covenantal love
rationale: Isaiah calls Israel and Jacob God's chosen servant and Abraham's offspring; Deuteronomy likewise describes Israel's choice as God's possession, grounded in divine love and His oath to the fathers.
source_text: But you, Israel, My servant Jacob whom I chose, offspring of Abraham whom I loved,

target_units.text: For you are a holy people unto the Lord your God; and the Lord your God has chosen you to be unto Him a people for His own possession, above all the nations upon the face of the earth.
The Lord preferred you and chose you, not because you were more numerous than all the nations, for you are the fewest of all the nations,

but because the Lord loved you, and kept the oath which He sware unto your fathers, the Lord brought you forth with a mighty hand and with an uplifted arm, and redeemed you out of the house of bondage, out of the hand of Pharaoh king of Egypt.

relationship: related divine taking and choosing of Israel
rationale: Isaiah describes God taking and calling His chosen servant from earth's extremities; Deuteronomy recalls God taking a nation from another nation and choosing the fathers' offspring in the exodus. The places and events of the taking differ.
source_text: whom I took hold of from the earth’s extremities, and from its lookout heights called you and said, ‘You are My servant; I chose you and did not abandon you’—

target_units.text: Or has God attempted to go and take unto Himself a nation from the midst of a nation, by trial, and by signs, and by wonders, and by war, and by a mighty hand, and by an uplifted arm, and by great visions, according to all that the Lord our God did in Egypt before your eyes?
That you might know that the Lord your God, He is God, and there is none beside Him.
Out of heaven His voice was made heard, to instruct you; and upon earth He showed you His great fire, and you heard His words out of the midst of the fire.
Because He loved your fathers, He chose their seed after them, even you, and Himself brought you forth out of Egypt by His great strength,

relationship: close reassurance not to fear because God is present
rationale: Isaiah grounds freedom from fear in God's presence, strength and help; Moses likewise tells Israel and Joshua not to fear because the Lord is with them and will not abandon them. Isaiah additionally specifies the righteous right hand.
source_text: do not fear, for I am with you; do not wander, for I am your God who strengthened you. I helped you and secured you with My righteous right hand.

target_units.text: Be courageous and strong; fear not, neither be fainthearted, neither be terrified before their face; for the Lord your God, who goes before you, is with you and among you. He will in no wise fail you, neither will He forsake you.

And Moses called Joshua, and said unto him before all Israel, Be courageous and strong; for you shall go before the face of this people into the land which the Lord sware unto our fathers to give unto them, and you shall give it unto them for an inheritance.
And the Lord who goes with you will not fail you, neither will He forsake you; fear not, neither be fainthearted.

relationship: parallel shame of opponents in the presence of divine help
rationale: Isaiah promises that opponents will be ashamed and abashed; Jeremiah describes the Lord with him as a strong fighter and his pursuers greatly shamed. Isaiah additionally promises their perishing, which this Jeremiah unit does not state.
source_text: Behold, all opposing you will be ashamed and abashed, for all your adversaries will be as though they did not exist and will perish.

target_units.text: And the Lord is with me like a strong fighter. Therefore they pursued and could not understand; they were greatly shamed, because they did not understand their dishonors, which will never be forgotten.

relationship: close search finding a formerly powerful enemy absent
rationale: Isaiah says those seeking their attackers will not find them, as though they did not exist; the psalmist sees an exalted ungodly person disappear and cannot find his place when searching. The individual and collective scopes differ.
source_text: You will seek them but certainly not find the people who insult you. For those warring against you will be as though they did not exist, and will not exist.

target_units.text: I saw an ungodly person raised high and lifting himself like the cedars of Lebanon.
I passed by, and behold, he was gone; I sought him, but his place could not be found.

relationship: close God holding the person's right hand
rationale: Isaiah describes God holding the addressee's right hand and speaking reassurance; the psalmist likewise says God grasped his right hand and guided him by counsel. The stated divine assistance is personal and specific.
source_text: For I am your God who holds your right hand and says to you, ‘Do not fear,

target_units.text: And I am continually with Thee; Thou didst grasp my right hand.
In Thy counsel Thou didst guide me, and with glory Thou didst receive me.

relationship: related reassurance to a little community
rationale: Isaiah's 'little Israel' is told not to fear in the continuing address from 41:13, because God helped and redeems it; Jesus likewise tells the little flock not to fear because the Father gives the kingdom. The community descriptions and promised gifts differ.
source_text: Jacob, little Israel. I helped you,’ says God who redeems you, Israel.

target_units.text: Do not fear, little flock, because your Father was pleased to give you the kingdom.

relationship: parallel empowerment for threshing and grinding opponents
rationale: Isaiah makes Israel like new saw-toothed wagon wheels that thresh mountains and grind hills; Micah gathers nations like threshing-floor sheaves and equips Zion with iron horns and bronze hooves to grind peoples. Instruments and objects differ within the shared threshing image.
source_text: Behold, I made you like new, saw-toothed wagon wheels for threshing. You will thresh mountains, grind hills fine, and make them like dust.

target_units.text: But they did not know the Lord’s thought or understand His counsel, for He gathered them like sheaves of a threshing floor.

Rise and thresh them, daughter of Zion, for I will make your horns iron and your hooves bronze. With them you will melt down nations and grind many peoples fine; you will dedicate their multitude to the Lord and their strength to the Lord of all the earth.

relationship: related winnowing and scattering by wind
rationale: After the mountains and hills are ground in 41:15, Isaiah describes winnowing followed by wind and storm scattering; the psalm likens the ungodly to chaff flung away by wind. The source does not itself name chaff in this sentence.
source_text: You will winnow, and wind will take them and a storm scatter them. But you will rejoice among Israel’s holy ones. And they will exult—

target_units.text: Not so the ungodly, not so, but like chaff which the wind flings away from the face of the earth.

relationship: related rejoicing among Israel's holy ones
rationale: Isaiah says the addressee will rejoice among Israel's holy ones; the psalm combines praise in their assembly, Israel's rejoicing and holy ones boasting in glory and rejoicing. Isaiah's plural holy ones is preserved rather than changed into a singular title for God.
source_text: You will winnow, and wind will take them and a storm scatter them. But you will rejoice among Israel’s holy ones. And they will exult—

target_units.text: Hallelujah. Sing a new song to the Lord, His praise in the assembly of holy ones.
Let Israel rejoice in the One who made it, and let Zion’s children exult in their King.
Let them praise His name in a chorus; with tambourine and psaltery let them make music to Him.
For the Lord takes pleasure in His people, and He will exalt the meek in salvation.
Holy ones will boast in glory and rejoice upon their beds.

relationship: parallel divine response to waterless thirst and need
rationale: Isaiah describes needy people seeking unavailable water and God hearing without abandoning them; the psalm describes hungry, thirsty wanderers in a waterless place who cry to the Lord and are rescued. Both join physical need with answered appeal.
source_text: the poor and needy. For they will seek water, and there will be none; their tongue dried from thirst. I am the Lord God; I will listen, the God of Israel, and will not abandon them,

target_units.text: They wandered in the wilderness, in a waterless place; they did not find a road to a city of habitation,
hungry and thirsty; their soul failed within them.
They cried to the Lord when they were afflicted, and He rescued them from their distresses,
and guided them into a straight way to travel to a city of habitation.
