Let them acknowledge to the Lord His mercies and His wonders to the sons of men,
for He filled an empty soul and filled a hungry soul with good things.

relationship: close wilderness transformed into abundant water
rationale: Isaiah promises rivers, springs and marshes in formerly thirsty land; the psalm likewise turns wilderness into lakes and waterless land into outlets, then settles hungry people there. The particular landscape terms differ.
source_text: but will open rivers on mountains and springs amid plains. I will make the wilderness marshes and the thirsty land watercourses,

target_units.text: He made a wilderness lakes of waters and waterless land outlets of waters,
and settled hungry people there, and they established a city of habitation,
and sowed fields and planted vineyards and produced a fruitful crop.

relationship: internal planting of cypress and myrtle in transformed land
rationale: Isaiah 41 includes cypress and myrtle among trees placed in waterless land; Isaiah 55 has cypress replace thorny shrub and myrtle replace fleabane. The named trees and restored growth correspond, while the prior conditions differ.
source_text: and will place cedar, box tree, myrtle, cypress, and white poplar in the waterless land,

target_units.text: And the cypress will rise in place of the thorny shrub, and the myrtle will rise in place of the fleabane; and the Lord will be for a name and for an everlasting sign, and will not fail.

relationship: close recognition that the Lord's hand made these things
rationale: Isaiah intends observers to know that the Lord's hand accomplished the renewed landscape; Job appeals to creatures and earth in asking who does not know that the Lord's hand made these things. Recognition of divine workmanship connects the passages.
source_text: so that they may see and know, consider and understand together that the Lord’s hand did all these things and Israel’s Holy One displayed them.

target_units.text: But ask the four-footed animals, to see whether they will tell you, and the birds of heaven, to see whether they will report to you.
Speak fully to the earth, to see whether it will tell you; and the fish of the sea will explain to you.
Who among all these did not know that the Lord’s hand made these things?
Is not the life of all living things in His hand, and the breath of every human being?

relationship: internal contrast between demanded prediction and God's announced fulfillment
rationale: Isaiah 41 challenges the claimants to announce former and coming things; Isaiah 46 identifies God as the One who announced last things before they occurred and whose counsel stands. The later assertion answers the kind of test posed here.
source_text: Let them approach and announce to you what will happen. Or say what the former things were, and we will apply our mind and know what the last things are; tell us also the coming things.

target_units.text: Remember the former things from eternity, for I am God, and there is none besides Me,
announcing the last things beforehand, before they came to be—and together they were fulfilled. I said, ‘All My counsel will stand, and I will do everything I have planned,’

relationship: close challenge concerning idols' ability to do good or harm
rationale: Isaiah challenges the claimants to do good and cause harm so observers may recognize their divinity; Jeremiah says not to fear handmade gods because they cannot do evil and no good is in them. This addresses the action clause alongside Isaiah's prediction challenge.
source_text: Announce to us the things coming at the end, and we will know that you are gods. Do good and cause harm, and we will marvel and see together.

target_units.text: They must be lifted and carried, because they will not take a step. Do not fear them, because they certainly will not do evil, and no good is in them.

relationship: related earthly origin of a manufactured god
rationale: Isaiah answers the challenged claimants' origin with earth and calls their choice an abomination; Wisdom describes a potter fashioning a futile god from the same clay as ordinary vessels. The earthly material exposes the supposed god's manufacture.
source_text: For where are you from, and where is your work from? From the earth! They chose you as an abomination.

target_units.text: For a potter, laboriously kneading soft earth, shapes each object for our service; from the same clay he fashioned alike vessels serving clean purposes and those serving the opposite; and the clay-worker decides the use of each kind.

With evil labor he also shapes a futile god from the same clay, though he himself, having come from earth a little before, will shortly go back to that from which he was taken, when the debt of his soul is demanded.

relationship: related peoples portrayed as potter's clay under superior power
rationale: Isaiah calls rulers to come and compares the addressees' trampling with clay under a potter; Jeremiah compares Israel in God's hands with clay reshaped by a potter. The shared political use of potter's clay preserves the difference between trampling and reshaping.
source_text: But I roused the one from the north and the one from the sun’s rising; they will be called by My name. Let rulers come, and like a potter’s clay, as a potter tramples clay, so you will be trampled.

target_units.text: And the vessel he was making fell apart in his hands, and again he made it another vessel, as pleased him to make.
And the Lord’s word came to me, saying:
Can I not shape you as this potter does, house of Israel? Behold, you are like the potter’s clay in My hands.

relationship: internal test of announcing events beforehand
rationale: Isaiah 41 asks who announced events earlier so their truth could be recognized and finds no predictor; Isaiah 48 says God announced and accomplished former things beforehand so they could not be credited to idols.
source_text: For who will announce the things from the beginning so we may know, and the earlier things so we may say, ‘They are true’? There is no one predicting, nor anyone hearing your words.

target_units.text: I announced the former things beforehand; they went out from My mouth and were heard. Suddenly I acted, and they arrived.
I know that you are stubborn, your neck an iron sinew and your forehead bronze.
I announced it to you long ago; before it came upon you I made you hear it. Do not say, ‘My idols did it,’ or say, ‘My carved and cast images commanded me.’

relationship: internal renewed comfort for Jerusalem
rationale: Isaiah 41 promises comfort to Jerusalem for a journey; Isaiah 40 commands comfort and speech to Jerusalem's heart because humiliation is fulfilled. The shared named city and promised comfort connect the sayings without substituting a different announcement for 41:27.
source_text: I will give Zion a beginning and comfort Jerusalem for a journey.

target_units.text: Comfort, comfort My people, says God.
You priests, speak to the heart of Jerusalem; comfort her. For her humiliation is fulfilled, her sin is loosed; for from the hand of the Lord she has received double for her sins.

relationship: parallel inability of handmade gods to answer
rationale: Isaiah finds no announcer among idols and says they cannot answer God's question about their origin; the psalm calls national idols human handiwork and says their mouths will not speak. The source's examination exposes the speechlessness described by the psalm.
source_text: For behold, there is no one from the nations, and none among their idols was an announcer. If I ask them, ‘Where are you from?’ they will certainly not answer Me.

target_units.text: The idols of the nations are silver and gold, works of human hands.
They have a mouth and will not speak; they have eyes and will not see.

relationship: related futility of makers and manufactured gods
rationale: Isaiah identifies makers and futile misleading; Jeremiah describes goldsmiths shamed by false, spiritless carvings and calls their works futile. The surrounding idol challenge supplies the particular setting for both accusations.
source_text: For there are those making you, and those misleading you do so in vain.”

target_units.text: Every human became foolish, without knowledge; every goldsmith was put to shame at his carved things, because they cast false things; there is no spirit in them.
They are futile, mocked works; at the time of their visitation they will perish.

relationship: explicit servant citation applied to Jesus
rationale: Matthew cites Isaiah's chosen servant, divine approval, Spirit and judgment for the nations as fulfilled in Jesus' ministry. Isaiah explicitly names Jacob and Israel in this unit; Matthew's citation does not repeat those names.
source_text: “Jacob is My servant; I will uphold him. Israel is My chosen one; My soul accepted him. I put My spirit upon him; he will bring judgment to the nations.

target_units.text: so that what was spoken through Isaiah the prophet might be fulfilled:
“Behold, My Servant whom I chose, My beloved in whom My soul was well pleased. I will put My Spirit upon Him, and He will proclaim justice to the nations.

relationship: explicit quotation of the servant's restraint of voice
rationale: Matthew's servant citation repeats the refusal to cry out or have His voice heard publicly. Isaiah says outside; Matthew specifies the streets and also denies quarrelling.
source_text: He will not cry out or raise his voice, nor will his voice be heard outside.

target_units.text: He will not quarrel or cry out, nor will anyone hear His voice in the streets.

relationship: explicit quotation of the bruised reed and smoking wick
rationale: Both preserve the bruised reed and smoldering wick and connect this restraint with judgment. Isaiah says judgment in truth; Matthew says justice brought forth to victory.
source_text: He will not crush a bruised reed or extinguish a smoking flax wick; rather, he will bring judgment in truth.

target_units.text: He will not break a bruised reed or extinguish a smoldering wick, until He brings justice forth to victory.

relationship: explicit quotation of the nations hoping in the servant's name
rationale: Matthew concludes its servant citation with nations hoping in His name, matching the source's final clause. It does not repeat this unit's promise that he will shine forth and not be broken.
source_text: He will shine forth and will not be broken until he sets judgment upon the earth, and nations will hope in his name.”

target_units.text: And nations will hope in His name.”

relationship: close Creator giving life and breath to humanity
rationale: Isaiah identifies God as maker of heaven, earth and its contents and giver of breath to its people; Paul likewise names the Maker of the world and Lord of heaven and earth who gives everyone life and breath.
source_text: Thus says the Lord God, who made heaven and fixed it in place, established the earth and its contents, and gives breath to the people upon it and spirit to those treading it:

target_units.text: The God who made the world and everything in it, being Lord of heaven and earth, does not dwell in sanctuaries made by hands.
Nor is He served by human hands as though He needed anything, since He Himself gives everyone life and breath and everything.

relationship: internal appointment as covenant and light for nations
rationale: Both describe God's servant appointed as a covenant for a people or race and a light for nations. Isaiah 49 additionally spells out restoration of Israel's dispersion and salvation to earth's extremity.
source_text: “I, the Lord God, called you in righteousness; I will hold your hand and strengthen you. I gave you as a covenant for a people, a light for nations,

target_units.text: and He said to me, “It is a great thing for you to be called My servant, to establish Jacob’s tribes and bring back Israel’s dispersion. Behold, I have appointed you as a covenant for a race, a light for nations, so that you may bring salvation to the earth’s extremity.”

relationship: related light-for-nations image applied to Jesus
rationale: Isaiah appoints the servant a light for nations; Simeon, holding Jesus, calls the salvation he has seen a light for revelation to nations and glory for Israel. Luke's setting gives the image a specified application.
source_text: “I, the Lord God, called you in righteousness; I will hold your hand and strengthen you. I gave you as a covenant for a people, a light for nations,

target_units.text: because my eyes have seen Thy salvation,
which Thou didst prepare in the sight of all peoples:
a light for revelation to the nations and glory for Thy people Israel.”

relationship: related mission of opening blind eyes and releasing captives
rationale: Isaiah joins sight for blind people with release from bonds and prison darkness; Jesus reads a mission of recovery of sight and release for captives and the oppressed. Luke's cited passage shares these motifs without being presented as a verbatim quotation of this unit.
source_text: to open blind people’s eyes, bring those bound out of bonds, and those sitting in darkness out of the prison house.

target_units.text: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon Me, because He anointed Me to proclaim good news to the poor. He has sent Me to proclaim release to captives and recovery of sight to the blind, to send the oppressed away in release,

relationship: internal refusal to give God's glory to another
rationale: Both directly state that God will not give His glory to another. Isaiah 42 additionally says He will not give His praiseworthy deeds to carved images, while Isaiah 48 connects the declaration with His profaned name.
source_text: I am the Lord God; this is My name. I will not give My glory to another or My praiseworthy deeds to carved images.

target_units.text: For My sake I will act for you, because My name is being profaned. I will not give My glory to another.

relationship: internal announcement preceding fulfillment
rationale: Isaiah 42 distinguishes former things arrived from new things disclosed before appearing; Isaiah 48 likewise says God announced former events before acting and before they arrived, preventing their attribution to idols.
source_text: Behold, the things from the beginning have arrived, and new things I will announce; before they spring up, they were disclosed to you.”

target_units.text: I announced the former things beforehand; they went out from My mouth and were heard. Suddenly I acted, and they arrived.
I know that you are stubborn, your neck an iron sinew and your forehead bronze.
I announced it to you long ago; before it came upon you I made you hear it. Do not say, ‘My idols did it,’ or say, ‘My carved and cast images commanded me.’

relationship: close new song and praise extending across the earth
rationale: Both summon a new song to the Lord and proclamation of His name and glory across the earth and peoples. Isaiah specifically includes seafarers, islands and their inhabitants.
source_text: Sing a new hymn to the Lord—its beginning: “Glorify His name from the earth’s extremity, you who go down to the sea and sail it, islands and their inhabitants.”

target_units.text: When the house was being built after the captivity; a song of David. Sing to the Lord a new song; sing to the Lord, all the earth.
Sing to the Lord; bless His name. Proclaim the good news of His salvation day after day.
Announce His glory among the nations, His wonders among all the peoples.

relationship: internal summons for the wilderness to rejoice
rationale: Both directly summon wilderness or desert places to rejoicing. Isaiah 42 names Kedar and Petra and their inhabitants; Isaiah 35 describes flowering desert places and the sight of God's glory.
source_text: Rejoice, wilderness and its villages, settlements and those inhabiting Kedar. Those inhabiting Petra will rejoice and cry out from the mountain tops.

target_units.text: Rejoice, thirsty wilderness! Let the wilderness exult and flower like a lily,
and the Jordan’s desert places will flower and exult. Lebanon’s glory and Carmel’s honor were given to her, and My people will see the Lord’s glory and God’s height.

relationship: parallel giving of glory to God among peoples
rationale: Isaiah predicts giving God glory and announcing His praiseworthy deeds in the islands; the psalm commands families of nations to bring the Lord glory and honor for His name.
source_text: They will give God glory and announce His praiseworthy deeds in the islands.

target_units.text: Bring to the Lord, families of nations; bring to the Lord glory and honor.
Bring to the Lord glory for His name; take up sacrifices and enter His courts.

relationship: close Lord shattering war and enemies
rationale: Isaiah says the Lord will crush war and cry mightily against His enemies; Exodus calls Him the One who shatters wars and praises His right hand shattering enemies. The supplied wording concerns His breaking war, not a substituted warrior title.
source_text: The Lord God of Powers will go out and crush war. He will rouse zeal and cry out mightily against His enemies.

target_units.text: The Lord shatters wars; the Lord is His name.
Pharaoh’s chariots and his host He has cast into the sea; chosen riders, officers, He has drowned in the Red Sea.
With the sea He covered them; they sank into the deep as a stone.
Thy right hand, O Lord, has been glorified in strength; Thy right hand, O Lord, has shattered enemies.

relationship: parallel divine silence ending in intervention
rationale: Isaiah's God says He was silent but will not remain silent and hold back; the psalm likewise moves from God's silence while wrongdoing continued to His announced rebuke. Isaiah's childbirth and drying imagery is additional.
source_text: “I was silent; surely I will not always be silent and hold back? I endured like a woman giving birth; I will astonish and dry up together.

target_units.text: These things you did, and I kept silent; you conceived the lawless thought that I would be like you. I will rebuke you and set it before your face.

relationship: related transformation of waters into dry territory
rationale: Isaiah turns rivers into islands and dries marshes; the psalm turns rivers into wilderness and water outlets into thirst. Both describe divine removal or transformation of watery places, with different resulting terrain.
source_text: I will turn rivers into islands and dry up marshes.

target_units.text: He made rivers a wilderness and outlets of waters thirst,
a fruitful land brine, because of the wickedness of those inhabiting it.

relationship: related opening of sight and movement from darkness to light
rationale: Isaiah promises guidance for blind people and darkness turned to light; Jesus commissions Paul to open people's eyes so they turn from darkness to light and from Satan's authority to God. Acts explicitly describes conversion, while Isaiah also supplies road imagery.
source_text: I will lead the blind on a road they did not know and make them tread paths they did not know. I will turn darkness into light for them and crooked places straight. These things I will do, and I will not abandon them.

target_units.text: rescuing you from the people and from the Gentiles, to whom I am sending you,

to open their eyes, so that they may turn from darkness to light and from Satan’s authority to God, so that they may receive forgiveness of sins and an allotted share among those sanctified by faith in Me.’

relationship: close shame of those trusting and worshiping images
rationale: Isaiah commands shame upon those trusting carved images and calling cast images their gods; the psalm likewise calls those bowing to carved images and boasting in idols to shame.
source_text: But they turned backward. Be utterly ashamed, you who trust carved images, who say to cast images, ‘You are our gods.’”

target_units.text: Let all who bow down to carved images be ashamed, those who boast in their idols. Bow down to Him, all His angels!

relationship: parallel call for unresponsive people to hear
rationale: Isaiah commands deaf people to listen and blind people to look and see; Jeremiah summons Jacob and Judah to hear while describing people with eyes that do not see and ears that do not hear.
source_text: Deaf people, listen; blind people, look up and see!

target_units.text: Announce these things to the house of Jacob, and let it be heard in Judah.
Hear these things now, foolish and senseless people: they have eyes and do not see; they have ears and do not hear.

relationship: related failure of spiritual perception among a people and its guides
rationale: Isaiah rebukes blind servants of God and deaf rulers; Jesus calls the Pharisees blind guides of blind people. The sensory diagnoses and groups differ, while both expose failed religious perception.
source_text: Who is blind except My servants, or deaf except those ruling them? God’s slaves have become blind.

target_units.text: Then the disciples came and said to Him, “Dost Thou know that the Pharisees stumbled when they heard this saying?”
He answered, “Every plant that My heavenly Father did not plant will be uprooted.
Leave them; they are blind guides of the blind. If a blind person guides a blind person, both will fall into a pit.”

relationship: close rebuke for seeing and hearing without understanding
rationale: Isaiah says the hearers saw but did not keep watch and had opened ears but did not listen; Jesus asks His disciples why their eyes and ears do not perceive and why they do not understand.
source_text: You saw often but did not keep watch; the ears were opened, but you did not listen.

target_units.text: Aware of this, He said to them, “Why are you reasoning that you have no bread? Do you not yet grasp or understand? Is your heart hardened?
Having eyes, do you not see? Having ears, do you not hear? And do you not remember,

relationship: related vindication of God amid human unfaithfulness
rationale: Isaiah says the Lord wished to be justified and magnify praise; Paul defends God's faithfulness and applies the saying that God is justified in His words. The comparison concerns divine vindication, preserving the source's actual praise language.
source_text: The Lord God wished to be justified and to magnify praise. And I saw,

target_units.text: For what if some were unfaithful? Will their unfaithfulness nullify God’s faithfulness?
May it never be! But let God be true, and every human being a liar, just as it is written, “So that Thou mayest be justified in Thy words, and wilt prevail when Thou art judged.”

relationship: parallel people becoming plunder without rescuing care
rationale: Isaiah describes people plundered with no rescuer or demand for their return; Ezekiel describes God's sheep plundered because their shepherds failed to seek them, followed by God's promised rescue. The flock image is Ezekiel's particular formulation.
source_text: and the people became plundered and despoiled. For the snare is in the storerooms everywhere and in houses together, where they hid them. They became plunder, and no one rescued the spoil; no one said, ‘Give it back!’

target_units.text: My sheep scattered because there were no shepherds and became food for all the field’s beasts.
My sheep scattered on every mountain and upon every high hill, and scattered over the whole face of the earth. There was no one seeking them out or turning them back.
Therefore, shepherds, hear the Lord’s word:

I live, says the Lord, the Lord: surely because My sheep became plunder and My sheep became food for all the plain’s beasts for lack of shepherds, and the shepherds did not seek out My sheep but fed themselves and did not feed My sheep—
because of this, shepherds,

thus says the Lord, the Lord: Behold, I am against the shepherds. I will require My sheep from their hands and turn them aside from shepherding My sheep. The shepherds will no longer feed them. I will rescue My sheep from their mouth, and they will no longer be food for them.

relationship: parallel God handing disobedient Israel to plunderers
rationale: Isaiah identifies God as the One who gave Jacob and Israel to plunder because they sinned and refused His ways; Judges likewise records Israel forsaking Him and His handing them to plunderers and enemies.
source_text: Who gave Jacob over to plunder and Israel to those despoiling him? Was it not God, against whom they sinned, refusing to walk in His ways or listen to His law?

target_units.text: The sons of Israel did evil before the Lord and served the Baalim.

They forsook the Lord, the God of their fathers, who had brought them out of the land of Egypt. They followed other gods from among the gods of the peoples around them, bowed down to them, and provoked the Lord.
They forsook the Lord and served Baal and the Astartes.

The Lord was greatly angered against Israel. He delivered them into the hand of plunderers, who plundered them; and He sold them into the hand of their enemies all around, so they could not stand before their enemies.
In everything in which they prostituted themselves, the Lord’s hand was against them for harm, as the Lord had spoken and as the Lord had sworn. He greatly afflicted them.

relationship: parallel severe judgment without the required response
rationale: Isaiah describes war and surrounding burning without understanding or taking it to heart; Amos describes sword, camps in fire and a firebrand rescued from burning, yet no return to God. The absent responses are expressed differently.
source_text: He brought His wrathful anger upon them; war overpowered them, as did those burning them all around. None of them understood, nor did they take it to soul.

target_units.text: “I sent death among you on Egypt’s road and killed your young men with the sword, along with the captivity of your horses. I brought your camps up in fire in My anger; yet not even so did you turn to Me,” says the Lord.
“I overthrew you as God overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah, and you became like a firebrand snatched from fire. Yet not even so did you turn to Me,” says the Lord.

relationship: related belonging expressed through calling by name
rationale: God calls Israel by name and claims it as His own; Jesus' shepherd figure calls his own sheep by name and leads them. The collective address and the individual sheep in the figure differ.
source_text: But now thus says the Lord God who made you, Jacob, who formed you, Israel: “Do not fear, for I redeemed you. I called you by your name; you are Mine.

target_units.text: To him the doorkeeper opens, and the sheep hear his voice. He calls his own sheep by name and leads them out.
When he has brought all his own out, he goes before them, and the sheep follow him, because they know his voice.

relationship: historical counterpart to safe passage through water
rationale: Isaiah promises God's presence and protection when His people cross waters; Exodus records the Lord opening the sea and Israel walking within it on dry ground between walls of water.
source_text: Even if you cross through water, I am with you, and rivers will not flood over you. Even if you pass through fire, you will certainly not be burned up; flame will not burn you up.

target_units.text: Moses stretched out his hand over the sea. The Lord drove the sea back with a violent south wind all night and made the sea dry. The water was split.
The sons of Israel entered the midst of the sea on dry ground, and the water was a wall for them on the right and a wall on the left.

relationship: narrative counterpart to unharmed presence amid fire
rationale: Isaiah promises that flame will not burn the people passing through fire; Daniel describes the Lord's angel joining the companions in the furnace and the fire neither touching nor distressing them.
source_text: Even if you cross through water, I am with you, and rivers will not flood over you. Even if you pass through fire, you will certainly not be burned up; flame will not burn you up.

target_units.text: An angel of the Lord descended into the furnace together with Azariah and his companions and shook the flame of fire out of the furnace.
He made the middle of the furnace like a dew-laden breeze whistling through. The fire did not touch them at all; it neither distressed nor troubled them.

relationship: related Egypt given as divine compensation
rationale: Isaiah names Egypt as an exchange on Israel's behalf; Ezekiel describes God giving Egypt to Babylon's king as wages in exchange for service against Tyre. Recipients and grounds differ, and Ezekiel does not supply Isaiah's Ethiopia and Soene clauses.
source_text: For I am the Lord your God, Israel’s Holy One, who saves you. I made Egypt your exchange, and Ethiopia and Soene on your behalf.

target_units.text: Thus says the Lord, the Lord: Behold, I give the land of Egypt to Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon. He will take her booty and strip her spoils; it will be wages for his force.
In exchange for his service, which he performed against Tyre, I have given him the land of Egypt. Thus says the Lord, the Lord:

relationship: related another person given in place of a favored recipient
rationale: Isaiah promises people and rulers on Israel's behalf; Proverbs describes the righteous escaping a hunt and the impious handed over in his place. Proverbs specifies moral categories that Isaiah does not assign to the exchanged rulers.
source_text: Since you became honored before Me, you were glorified, and I loved you. I will give many people on your behalf and rulers for your head.

target_units.text: The righteous escapes from the hunt, but the impious is handed over in his place.

relationship: close gathering of the redeemed from east and west
rationale: Isaiah promises to bring offspring from the east and gather the people from the west; the psalm calls the redeemed to thanksgiving and says God gathered them from countries including east and west, with north and sea also named.
source_text: Do not fear, for I am with you. From the east I will bring your offspring, and from the west I will gather you.

target_units.text: Let those redeemed by the Lord say so, those He redeemed from the enemy’s hand.
He gathered them from the countries, from east and west and north and the sea.

relationship: internal return of sons and daughters from abroad
rationale: Isaiah 43 commands distant regions to bring God's sons and daughters; Isaiah 49 describes a signal to nations and islands followed by sons brought in the bosom and daughters carried on shoulders. The manner of their return is developed differently.
source_text: I will say to the north, ‘Bring them,’ and to the southwest, ‘Do not hinder. Bring My sons from a distant land and My daughters from the earth’s extremities,

target_units.text: Thus says the Lord: “Behold, I lift My hand toward nations and will raise My signal toward islands. They will bring your sons in their bosom and carry your daughters on shoulders,

relationship: related community bearing God's name
rationale: Isaiah includes all called by God's name in the gathering of His formed people; Jeremiah's community appeals to the fact that God's name has been called over them and asks Him not to forget them. The shared name expresses their belonging to God.
source_text: all who are called by My name.’ For in My glory I fashioned him, formed him, and made him,

target_units.text: Wilt Thou be like a sleeping man, or like a man unable to save? Yet Thou art among us, Lord, and Thy name has been called over us; do not forget us.

relationship: close sensory blindness and deafness of Jacob's people
rationale: Isaiah describes a blind people and deaf people possessing ears; Jeremiah addresses Jacob and Judah as having eyes without seeing and ears without hearing. Both portray the community's failure of perception through the same sensory organs.
source_text: and I brought out a blind people, and their eyes are likewise blind, and deaf people who have ears.

target_units.text: Announce these things to the house of Jacob, and let it be heard in Judah.
Hear these things now, foolish and senseless people: they have eyes and do not see; they have ears and do not hear.

relationship: internal judicial challenge to announce and substantiate events
rationale: Isaiah 43 asks assembled nations for announcements and truthful witnesses; Isaiah 41 challenges the claimants to announce former and coming things so their claims to divinity can be tested. Both frame knowledge of events as evidence in the dispute.
source_text: All nations were gathered together, and rulers from them will assemble. Who will announce these things, or who will announce to you the things from the beginning? Let them bring their witnesses, be justified, and speak true things.

target_units.text: Let them approach and announce to you what will happen. Or say what the former things were, and we will apply our mind and know what the last things are; tell us also the coming things.
Announce to us the things coming at the end, and we will know that you are gods. Do good and cause harm, and we will marvel and see together.

relationship: parallel knowledge that the Lord is the only God
rationale: Isaiah appoints witnesses so they may know and believe God's identity and denies any other god before or after Him; Deuteronomy describes God's acts so Israel may know He is God and there is none beside Him.
source_text: Become witnesses for Me—and I too am a witness, says the Lord God, and the servant whom I chose—so that you may know, believe, and understand that I am. Before Me no other god came to be, nor will there be one after Me.

target_units.text: Or has God attempted to go and take unto Himself a nation from the midst of a nation, by trial, and by signs, and by wonders, and by war, and by a mighty hand, and by an uplifted arm, and by great visions, according to all that the Lord our God did in Egypt before your eyes?
That you might know that the Lord your God, He is God, and there is none beside Him.

relationship: related belief in 'I am' through disclosed events
rationale: Isaiah links witness, knowledge and belief with God's declaration 'I am'; Jesus says He tells events beforehand so that, when they happen, His hearers may believe 'I am.' The speakers and immediate disclosed events are distinguished.
source_text: Become witnesses for Me—and I too am a witness, says the Lord God, and the servant whom I chose—so that you may know, believe, and understand that I am. Before Me no other god came to be, nor will there be one after Me.

target_units.text: From now on I tell you before it happens, so that when it happens you may believe that I am.

relationship: close declaration of no Savior apart from the Lord
rationale: Both identify the speaker as the Lord God and expressly deny anyone who saves apart from Him. Hosea additionally recalls creation and the exodus.
source_text: I am God, and apart from Me there is no one who saves.

target_units.text: But I am the Lord your God, who establishes heaven and creates earth, whose hands created all heaven’s host. I did not display them to you so that you should follow them. I brought you up from Egypt’s land; you shall know no god except Me, and there is none who saves apart from Me.

relationship: related exclusive claim concerning salvation
rationale: Isaiah says no one saves apart from God; Peter names Jesus Christ and says salvation is in no one else and no other saving name is given. Acts makes its particular application to Jesus explicit.
source_text: I am God, and apart from Me there is no one who saves.

target_units.text: let it be known to all of you and to all the people of Israel that in the name of Jesus Christ the Nazarene, whom you crucified, whom God raised from the dead—in Him this man stands before you in good health.
He is the stone despised by you, the builders, which has become the cornerstone.
Salvation is in no one else, for there is no other name under heaven given among human beings by which we must be saved.”

relationship: related appointment of a people as witnesses
rationale: Isaiah's God calls the people witnesses to His announced and saving acts; Jesus tells His chosen apostles they will be His witnesses from Jerusalem to earth's end. Isaiah additionally declares God Himself a witness.
source_text: I announced and saved; I reproached, and there was no foreign one among you. You are witnesses for Me, and I too am a witness, says the Lord God,

target_units.text: But you will receive power when the Holy Spirit comes upon you, and you will be My witnesses in Jerusalem and [in] all Judea and Samaria, and to the end of the earth.”

relationship: close impossibility of rescue from God's hand
rationale: Both explicitly deny that anyone can deliver or rescue from God's hands. Isaiah continues by asking who can reverse His action; Deuteronomy names His power to kill, make alive, strike and heal.
source_text: still from the beginning. No one rescues from My hands. I will act, and who will turn it back?”

target_units.text: See, see that I am, and there is no god beside Me. I will put to death, and make alive; I will smite, and I will heal; and there is none that shall deliver out of My hands.

relationship: parallel Israel's Redeemer acting against Babylon
rationale: Isaiah's Redeemer promises intervention in Babylon for the people's sake; Jeremiah names their strong Redeemer and says He will judge His adversaries and provoke Babylon's inhabitants. The ships and fleeing in Isaiah are not repeated by Jeremiah.
source_text: Thus says the Lord God who redeems you, Israel’s Holy One: “For your sake I will send to Babylon and rouse all who flee, and Chaldeans will be bound in ships.

target_units.text: Thus says the Lord: Israel’s sons and Judah’s sons have been oppressed together. All who captured them oppressed them, because they did not want to release them.
The One redeeming them is strong; the Lord Almighty is His name. He will judge a case against His adversaries, to remove the land, and He will provoke Babylon’s inhabitants.

relationship: historical counterpart of a path through the sea
rationale: Isaiah identifies the Lord as giving a way through sea and strong water; Exodus records His opening the sea so Israel crosses on dry ground. The narrative supplies the particular sea-passage pattern recalled by the description.
source_text: Thus says the Lord, who gives a way in the sea and a path in strong water,

target_units.text: Moses stretched out his hand over the sea. The Lord drove the sea back with a violent south wind all night and made the sea dry. The water was split.
The sons of Israel entered the midst of the sea on dry ground, and the water was a wall for them on the right and a wall on the left.

relationship: historical counterpart of the destruction of chariots and horsemen
rationale: Isaiah describes chariots, horse and mighty host brought out and finally extinguished; Exodus describes Pharaoh's horses, chariots and riders entering the sea and being covered, with none remaining. The sleep and wick metaphors are Isaiah's own images.
source_text: who brought out chariots and a horse and a mighty host: But they fell asleep and will not rise; they were extinguished like an extinguished flax wick.

target_units.text: The Egyptians pursued them, and all Pharaoh’s horses, the chariots, and the riders entered after them into the midst of the sea.
During the morning watch, the Lord looked on the Egyptians’ camp in a pillar of fire and cloud and threw the Egyptians’ camp into confusion.
He bound the axles of their chariots and drove them with force. The Egyptians said, “Let us flee from Israel, for the Lord is fighting for them against the Egyptians.”
And the Lord said to Moses, “Stretch out your hand over the sea, and let the water return and cover the Egyptians, both their chariots and their riders.”
Moses stretched out his hand over the sea, and toward daybreak the water returned to its place. The Egyptians fled beneath the water, and the Lord shook the Egyptians into the midst of the sea.
The water returned and covered the chariots, the riders, and all Pharaoh’s force that had entered the sea after them. Not one of them remained.

relationship: related movement of attention beyond former things
rationale: Isaiah commands not remembering or pondering former things before announcing a new divine work; Paul describes forgetting what is behind and stretching toward the goal ahead. The former things and the future object differ.
source_text: “Do not remember the first things or ponder the ancient ones.

target_units.text: Brothers, I do not consider myself to have taken hold. But one thing: forgetting the things behind and stretching forward to the things ahead,
I press on toward the goal for the prize of the upward calling of God in Christ Jesus.

relationship: internal joining of wilderness water and a new road
rationale: Isaiah 43 promises a wilderness way and rivers in waterless land; Isaiah 35 likewise describes water bursting in wilderness, thirsty land becoming springs, and a Holy Way for the scattered.
source_text: Behold, I am doing new things which will now spring up, and you will know them. I will make a way in the wilderness and rivers in the waterless land.

target_units.text: Then the lame person will leap like a deer, and the tongue of those with difficulty speaking will be clear, for water burst out in the wilderness and a ravine in a thirsty land,
the waterless place will become marshes, and a water spring will be in the thirsty land. There will be birds’ gladness, a dwelling of reeds and marshes.
There will be a clean road, called a Holy Way. No unclean person will ever pass there, nor will there be an unclean way there; the scattered will walk upon it and will certainly not wander.

relationship: parallel praise offered by wild creatures
rationale: Isaiah says wild beasts, sirens and ostrich daughters will bless God because He gives wilderness water; the psalm summons wild animals, cattle, creeping things and birds to praise His name. The species and the stated grounds differ.
source_text: The field’s wild beasts will bless Me, sirens and daughters of ostriches, because I gave water in the wilderness and rivers in the waterless land to give drink to My chosen race,

target_units.text: Praise the Lord from the earth, dragons and all deeps,
fire, hail, snow, ice, storm wind—all fulfilling His word,
mountains and all hills, fruit-bearing trees and all cedars,
wild animals and all cattle, creeping things and winged birds,
kings of the earth and all peoples, rulers and all judges of the earth,
young men and young women, old people with younger people.
Let them praise the Lord’s name, for His name alone was exalted; His praise is over earth and heaven.

relationship: close acquired people appointed to proclaim divine praise
rationale: Isaiah identifies God's acquired people as those who recount His praiseworthy deeds; First Peter likewise calls its addressees a people for God's possession so that they proclaim His excellences.
source_text: My people, whom I acquired to recount My praiseworthy deeds.

target_units.text: But you are a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for God’s possession, so that you may proclaim the excellences of Him who called you out of darkness into His marvelous light.

relationship: related divine denial of having burdened Israel
rationale: Isaiah's God says He did not make Israel toil; Micah's God asks how He grieved or troubled the people and recalls their redemption. This compares the labor clause without reversing Isaiah's opening statement that God did not call Jacob now.
source_text: I did not call you now, Jacob, nor did I make you toil, Israel.

target_units.text: “My people, what have I done to you? How have I grieved you, or how have I troubled you? Answer Me!
For I brought you up from Egypt’s land and redeemed you from the house of slavery. I sent Moses, Aaron and Miriam before you.

relationship: related challenge concerning animal offerings as service to God
rationale: Isaiah says the sheep offerings were not for God and the sacrifices did not glorify Him; the psalm refuses supplied calves and goats, declares God's ownership of all animals and calls instead for a sacrifice of praise.
source_text: The sheep for your whole burnt offering were not for Me, nor did you glorify Me with your sacrifices, nor did I make you toil with frankincense.

target_units.text: I will not rebuke you concerning your sacrifices; your burnt offerings are continually before Me.
I will not receive calves from your house or young goats from your flocks.
For all the forest’s wild animals are Mine, beasts on the mountains and cattle.
I know all the birds of heaven, and the field’s beauty is with Me.
If I become hungry, I will certainly not tell you, for the inhabited world and its fullness are Mine.
Will I eat bulls’ flesh or drink goats’ blood?
Sacrifice a sacrifice of praise to God and pay your vows to the Most High.

relationship: parallel rejection of God's supposed need for animal food
rationale: Isaiah says God did not desire the sacrifices' fat; the psalm says the world is His and asks whether He eats bulls' flesh or drinks goats' blood. Both challenge the idea that sacrificial food meets a divine need.
source_text: You did not acquire incense for Me with silver, nor did I desire the fat of your sacrifices; instead, amid your sins and wrongdoings I stood over you.

target_units.text: If I become hungry, I will certainly not tell you, for the inhabited world and its fullness are Mine.
Will I eat bulls’ flesh or drink goats’ blood?

relationship: close promise to forgive and no longer remember sins
rationale: Isaiah's God wipes out lawless acts and will not remember; Jeremiah's new-covenant promise likewise joins mercy toward injustices with sins remembered no more.
source_text: I am, I am the One who wipes out your lawless acts, and I will certainly not remember.

target_units.text: And they will certainly not teach each his fellow citizen or his brother, saying, Know the Lord, because they will all know Me, from their least to their greatest. I will be merciful toward their injustices and certainly remember their sins no more.

relationship: related confession of sins and restoration to right standing
rationale: Isaiah directs the addressee to state lawless acts so as to be justified; First John connects confession of sins with God's forgiveness and cleansing from unrighteousness. The stated outcomes are related but differently expressed.
source_text: But you, remember, and let us be judged. You, state your lawless acts first, so that you may be justified.

target_units.text: If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us.
If we confess our sins, He is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.

relationship: parallel acknowledgment of ancestral lawlessness
rationale: Isaiah says the first fathers and their rulers acted lawlessly against God; the psalmist acknowledges sin with the fathers and recalls their failure to understand and remember God's deeds in Egypt. Isaiah does not specify that particular ancestral episode here.
source_text: Your first fathers and their rulers acted lawlessly against Me,

target_units.text: We sinned with our fathers; we acted lawlessly and unjustly.
Our fathers in Egypt did not understand Thy wonders; they did not remember the abundance of Thy mercy and provoked Thee while going up in the Red Sea.

relationship: historical counterpart of sanctuary defilement and national judgment
rationale: Isaiah links rulers defiling holy things with Jacob handed to destruction and Israel to reproach; Chronicles describes leaders, priests and people defiling the Lord's house, rejecting His messengers and being handed to the Chaldeans.
source_text: and the rulers defiled My holy things, and I gave Jacob over to destruction and Israel to reproach.”

target_units.text: All the distinguished men of Judah, the priests, and the people of the land multiplied breaches of faith in the nations’ abominations and defiled the Lord’s house in Jerusalem.
The Lord, the God of their fathers, sent through prophets, rising early and sending His messengers, because He spared His people and His sanctuary.
They kept sneering at His messengers, treating His words as nothing, and mocking His prophets, until the Lord’s anger rose among His people, until there was no healing.

He brought against them a king of the Chaldeans, who killed their young men with the sword in the house of his sanctuary and did not spare Zedekiah. They had no mercy on their virgins and carried away their elders. He handed everything into their hands.

relationship: internal repeated naming of God's chosen servant
rationale: Both name Israel and Jacob as God's servant and chosen people. The recurring address identifies the people receiving the assurance without importing a different servant identity into this unit.
source_text: “But now listen, My servant Jacob, and Israel whom I chose.

target_units.text: But you, Israel, My servant Jacob whom I chose, offspring of Abraham whom I loved,

relationship: related divine formation from the womb and choice for service
rationale: Isaiah addresses chosen Jacob and Israel as formed from the womb; Jeremiah is told that God knew and consecrated him before his birth and appointed him a prophet. The corporate people and the individual prophet are distinct recipients.
source_text: Thus says the Lord God who made you and formed you from the womb: You will yet be helped. Do not fear, My servant Jacob and beloved Israel whom I chose.

target_units.text: The Lord’s word came to me, saying,
Before I formed you in the belly, I know you; before you came out of the womb, I have consecrated you. I have appointed you a prophet to nations.

relationship: close promise of God's Spirit upon descendants
rationale: Isaiah promises His Spirit upon the people's offspring and blessings upon their children; Joel promises an outpouring of His Spirit and prophecy by sons and daughters, extending also to male and female slaves.
source_text: For I will give water in thirst to those traveling through waterless land. I will place My spirit upon your offspring and My blessings upon your children,

target_units.text: “And it shall be after these things, that I will pour out of My Spirit upon all flesh; and your sons and your daughters shall prophesy, your elders shall dream dreams, and your young men shall see visions.
Even upon male slaves and female slaves in those days I will pour out of My Spirit.

relationship: related joining of thirst, water and the Spirit
rationale: Isaiah joins water for thirsty travelers with the Spirit placed upon offspring; Jesus invites thirsty people to drink, speaks of living water and, as John explains, means the Spirit believers will receive. John explicitly interprets its water image; Isaiah places the two promises alongside one another.
source_text: For I will give water in thirst to those traveling through waterless land. I will place My spirit upon your offspring and My blessings upon your children,

target_units.text: On the last day, the great day of the feast, Jesus stood and cried out, saying, “If anyone thirsts, let him come to Me and drink.
The one who believes in Me—as the Scripture said, rivers of living water will flow from his belly.”
He said this concerning the Spirit, whom those who believed in Him were about to receive; for the Spirit was not yet, because Jesus had not yet been glorified.

relationship: parallel flourishing through proximity to water
rationale: Isaiah compares the offspring's growth to grass amid water and a willow beside flowing water; the psalm compares the blessed person to a tree beside water outlets with fruit and an unfailing leaf. The plants and recipients differ within the shared growth image.
source_text: and they will spring up like grass amid water and like a willow beside flowing water.

target_units.text: He will be like the tree planted beside the outlets of waters, which will give its fruit in its season, and whose leaf will not fall off; and everything he does will be prospered.

relationship: related confession of belonging to the Lord
rationale: Isaiah describes people declaring and inscribing that they belong to God in the names of Jacob and Israel; Zechariah describes the tested remnant answering God's 'My people' with 'The Lord is my God.' Both express acknowledged belonging, without matching the inscriptions.
source_text: One will say, ‘I belong to God’; another will cry out in Jacob’s name; another will inscribe, ‘I belong to God,’ in Israel’s name.”

target_units.text: I will lead the third through fire, refine them with fire as silver is refined and test them as gold is tested. He will call on My name, and I will listen to him and say, ‘This is My people,’ and he will say, ‘The Lord is my God.’”

relationship: internal declaration of divine priority and enduring existence
rationale: Isaiah 44 says God is first and after these things; Isaiah 48 says He is first and forever. Both assert His encompassing priority and continuance, preserving the supplied wording rather than replacing it with a standard first-and-last formula.
source_text: Thus says God, Israel’s King, who rescued him, God Sabaoth: “I am first, and I am after these things; apart from Me there is no God.

target_units.text: Listen to Me, Jacob and Israel whom I call. I am first, and I am for ever,

relationship: internal divine incomparability demonstrated by announcing events
rationale: Both deny a rival like God and connect His uniqueness with announcement of what is coming. Isaiah 44 challenges rivals to announce events before arrival; Isaiah 46 says He announces final things beforehand and His counsel stands.
source_text: Who is like Me? Let him stand, call out, and prepare for Me, from when I made humankind for eternity. Let them announce to you the coming things before they arrive.

target_units.text: Remember the former things from eternity, for I am God, and there is none besides Me,
announcing the last things beforehand, before they came to be—and together they were fulfilled. I said, ‘All My counsel will stand, and I will do everything I have planned,’

relationship: internal witnesses to God's unique identity
rationale: Isaiah 44 asks the witnesses whether any God exists apart from Him and recalls His announcements; Isaiah 43 names the people witnesses to His announced and saving acts and denies other gods. This comparison concerns the witness and identity clauses.
source_text: Do not cover yourselves. Did you not hear from the beginning, and did I not announce it to you? You are witnesses whether there is a God apart from Me; there were none then.”

target_units.text: Become witnesses for Me—and I too am a witness, says the Lord God, and the servant whom I chose—so that you may know, believe, and understand that I am. Before Me no other god came to be, nor will there be one after Me.
I am God, and apart from Me there is no one who saves.
I announced and saved; I reproached, and there was no foreign one among you. You are witnesses for Me, and I too am a witness, says the Lord God,

relationship: parallel futility of hope in crafted gods
rationale: Isaiah calls image makers futile and their pleasing products unable to help; Wisdom calls hope in dead things wretched and identifies handmade objects called gods. Both expose the gap between craftsmanship and divine assistance.
source_text: All who fashion and carve are futile, making what pleases them, things that will not help them. But they will be ashamed—

target_units.text: But wretched are those whose hopes rest in dead things, who called the works of human hands gods: gold and silver, exercises of craftsmanship, likenesses of living creatures, or a useless stone, the work of an ancient hand.

relationship: parallel craftsman fashioning a futile god
rationale: Isaiah condemns fashioning a god and carving useless things; Wisdom describes a potter forming a futile god from the same clay used for ordinary vessels. The materials and crafts differ, while the manufactured deity's futility is explicit in both.
source_text: all who fashion a god and carve useless things,

target_units.text: For a potter, laboriously kneading soft earth, shapes each object for our service; from the same clay he fashioned alike vessels serving clean purposes and those serving the opposite; and the clay-worker decides the use of each kind.

With evil labor he also shapes a futile god from the same clay, though he himself, having come from earth a little before, will shortly go back to that from which he was taken, when the debt of his soul is demanded.

relationship: internal contrast of weakened maker and inexhaustible Creator
rationale: Isaiah's idol craftsman hungers and grows weak despite his strong arm; Isaiah 40 says God will not hunger or grow weary and gives strength to hungry people. The contrast separates the human maker's dependence from the Creator's sustaining power.
source_text: For a craftsman sharpened iron, worked it with an adze, bored it with a drill, and worked it with his strong arm. He will hunger and grow weak and certainly not drink water. Having selected

target_units.text: And now, did you not know, if you have not heard? God is eternal, the God who fashioned the earth’s extremities. He will not hunger or grow weary, and His understanding cannot be discovered.
He gives strength to the hungry, and grief to those who are not in pain.

relationship: close wooden human image installed in a dwelling

rationale: Isaiah describes eyes and heart darkened from perception in the idol-making account; Paul describes futile thoughts and a darkened heart as people exchange divine glory for images of mortal beings. Paul develops the pattern as refusal to honor the known God.

because he did not know the One who formed him, who breathed into him an active soul and breathed in a life-giving spirit.

rationale: Isaiah reminds formed Jacob and Israel of servant status and commands Israel not to forget God; Deuteronomy warns not to forget the God who brought them from Egypt and commands service to Him. The direction of remembering is the people's duty in both.
source_text: “Remember these things, Jacob and Israel, for you are My servant. I formed you as My servant; and you, Israel, do not forget Me.

rationale: Isaiah joins sins and lawless acts wiped away with the command to turn back to God and the promise of redemption; Peter likewise commands repentance and turning back so sins may be wiped away. The cloud and mist imagery belongs to Isaiah.

rationale: Isaiah summons heaven, earth's foundations, mountains and trees to joy over God's mercy and redemption of Israel; the psalm summons heavens, earth and woodland trees to rejoice before God's coming judgment. The shared cosmic praise has distinct stated occasions.
source_text: Rejoice, heavens, because God had mercy on Israel! Sound trumpets, earth’s foundations! Cry out joy, mountains, hills and all their trees! For God redeemed Jacob, and Israel will be glorified.

rationale: Isaiah's God says He stretched heaven alone; Job likewise attributes stretching heaven to God alone. Both exclude a companion maker in this particular act, while their adjoining earth and sea descriptions differ.

rationale: Isaiah announces inhabited Jerusalem, rebuilt Judean cities and deserted places springing up; Zechariah announces God's compassionate return to Jerusalem, His house rebuilt and cities overflowing with good things. Both promise restored city life under God's action.

relationship: historical counterpart to God's drying of deep waters
rationale: Isaiah's God declares the abyss desolate and its rivers dry; the psalm recalls His rebuke drying the Red Sea and His guidance through the deep as wilderness. The psalm supplies a concrete past act corresponding to the divine authority over deep water.

relationship: historical counterpart of Cyrus commissioned for Jerusalem's temple
rationale: Isaiah names Cyrus, says he will do God's wishes and promises Jerusalem and the holy house's foundation; Ezra records God stirring Cyrus and the king's proclamation that God commissioned him to build His house in Jerusalem. Isaiah's actual instruction to Cyrus is to understand.
source_text: He tells Cyrus to understand, and says, ‘He will do all My wishes.’ He says to Jerusalem, ‘You will be rebuilt, and I will lay the foundation of My holy house.’”

target_units.text: In the first year of Cyrus king of the Persians, so that the Lord’s word through Jeremiah’s mouth might be fulfilled, the Lord stirred the spirit of Cyrus king of the Persians. He ordered a proclamation throughout his kingdom, also in writing, saying:
“Thus says Cyrus king of the Persians: The Lord, God of heaven, has given me all the kingdoms of the earth, and He has charged me to build Him a house in Jerusalem in Judea.
Who among you belongs to any of His people? His God will be with him, and he will go up to Jerusalem in Judea. Let him build the house of the God of Israel—He is the God in Jerusalem.

relationship: narrative counterpart of the temple foundation laid
rationale: Isaiah promises that God will lay the foundation of His holy house; Ezra records the builders laying the Lord's house's foundation and priests, Levites and people celebrating it. This connection focuses on the foundation itself rather than Cyrus's proclamation.
